# Everyday_technology claim verification checklist

> Generated by `npm run verify:report` from `content/`. Do not edit by hand; record results with the commands below and regenerate.

**Progress:** 0 / 619 claims fully verified · 0 verified, 801 unverified, 0 incorrect, 0 unsupported (801 claim–source checks).

## How to verify

1. Open the source URL. Each section below is one source page with every claim that cites it.
2. For each claim, find the sentence on the page that supports it. Numbers must match (rounding like "about" is fine; a different figure is not).
3. Record the result (or fill in the CSV and run `npm run verify:import-csv -- docs/verification/everyday_technology.csv --by "Your Name"`):
   - **verified**: the page states it. Paste the supporting sentence as the quote.
   - **unsupported**: the page does not say it. Find a better source or change the claim.
   - **incorrect**: the page (or better evidence) contradicts it. The card/question must be revised in a new revision.
4. A level can only be published when every claim it states or teaches is verified against every source it cites. `npm run validate:content` enforces this.

"Pre-check" notes were written while drafting. They point at what to look at closely. They are not verification.

"Fact-check" results come from an automated check against independent sources found by web search (not the cited page, which couldn't be opened). A **corrected** or **disputed** claim was reworded to match those sources; the old wording is shown. They are not verification either: the cited page still has to be checked.

- **Tested by:**

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. fueleconomy.gov (All-Electric Vehicles) says EVs are propelled by electric motors powered by rechargeable battery packs. Sources: https://www.fueleconomy.gov/feg/evtech.shtml

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.computer_chip_growth`: unverified

> **Claim:** From the 4004's 2,300 transistors (1971) to the M1's 16 billion (2020) is a rise of about 7 million times: almost 23 doublings in 49 years, about one every two years.

- **Concept:** Moore's law (`concept.everyday_technology.computer_moores_law`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L53 “The Microchip” · `card.everyday_technology.053.c1` (text): A 2020 chip holds about 7 million times the switches of a 1971 one. / Intel's 4004 of 1971, the first commercially available microprocessor, had 2,300 transistors. Apple's M1 chip, announced in November 2020, has 16 billion. What exactly is a transistor, and how did so many squeeze onto one chip?
  - L53 “The Microchip” · `card.everyday_technology.053.c4` (fact): Moore's law is an observation, not a law of nature. / In 1965 Gordon Moore, who later co-founded Intel, predicted the number of parts on a chip would double every year. In 1975 he revised it to every two years. Nothing in physics forces it: chipmakers turned it into a target and kept chasing it. From 2,300 to 16 billion is almost 23 doublings in 49 years, about one every two years.
- **Tested by:**
  - L53 `question.everyday_technology.053.q2`: Why is Moore's law about chip transistor counts called an observation rather than a law of nature? → **It is a trend the industry chased, not something physics forces**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Arithmetic from corroborated inputs: 16,000,000,000 / 2,300 = 6.96 million; log2(6.96 million) = 22.7 doublings; 49 / 22.7 = 2.2 years each. Sources: https://spectrum.ieee.org/chip-hall-of-fame-intel-4004-microprocessor, https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20201110006071/en/Apple-Unleashes-M1

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.selfdriving_levels_3_to_5`: unverified

> **Claim:** At SAE Level 3 the car drives in limited conditions but the driver must take over when asked; Level 4 needs no takeover within its limits; Level 5 drives anywhere.

- **Concept:** SAE levels of driving automation (`concept.everyday_technology.selfdriving_levels`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L39 “Self-Driving Cars” · `card.everyday_technology.039.c3` (comparison): SAE's levels: who is driving?: Levels 0-2 (You are driving, even when features help; You must supervise all the time) vs Level 3 (The car drives in limited conditions; You must take over when it asks) vs Levels 4-5 (Level 4 needs no takeover within its limits; Level 5 would drive anywhere)
  - L39 “Self-Driving Cars” · `card.everyday_technology.039.c4` (fact): In 2023, California approved a Level 3 system for sale to the public. / On June 8, 2023, the state approved Mercedes-Benz Drive Pilot: highways only, daylight only, up to 40 mph, and the driver must stay behind the wheel to take over when prompted. Britannica noted that, as of 2025, no car was fully autonomous. This field moves fast, so the date on any claim matters.
- **Tested by:**
  - L39 `question.everyday_technology.039.q2`: A car drives itself on the highway but asks you to take over when it reaches its limits. Which SAE level is that? → **Level 3**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. SAE J3016 summary (search of ANSI/SAE descriptions): Level 3 expects the human to respond to a request to intervene; Level 4 performs the fallback itself in limited conditions; Level 5 is unconditional. Sources: https://blog.ansi.org/ansi/sae-levels-driving-automation-j-3016-2021/

## Human Efficiency (Body Physics: Motion to Metabolism, 2nd ed.) (Open Oregon Educational Resources)

- **Source:** `source.bodyphysics_human_efficiency`
- **URL:** https://openoregon.pressbooks.pub/bodyphysics2ed/chapter/locomotive-efficiency/
- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.body_efficiency_heat`: unverified

> **Claim:** At best the human body turns only about a quarter of its food energy into motion; most becomes heat, and most of the time the useful share is far lower.

- **Concept:** Energy changes form (`concept.everyday_technology.energy_conservation`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L2 “What Energy Is” · `card.everyday_technology.002.c3` (text): Energy never vanishes. It changes jobs. / Energy can't be created or destroyed, only changed from one form into another. Your breakfast holds chemical energy, and your body turns it into motion when you walk or play. But even at its best, your body turns only about a quarter of that energy into motion, and most of the rest becomes heat. That's why exercise warms you up. Nothing was lost; it just changed form.
- **Tested by:**
  - L2 `question.everyday_technology.002.q2`: After a run, where did most of your breakfast's energy go? → **Most of it became heat**
  - L5 `question.everyday_technology.005.q3`: Level 2 said energy is never destroyed. In an old bulb, where did about 90% of the energy go? → **It became heat**
  - L12 `question.everyday_technology.012.q3`: A coal plant turns only about a third of its fuel's energy into electricity. Where does the rest go? → **It ends up as waste heat**
  - L21 `question.everyday_technology.021.q3`: Level 2 said energy can't be created. How does a pulley system that cuts your pulling force obey that rule? → **You pull more rope, so the work stays the same**
  - L24 `question.everyday_technology.024.q3`: Level 2 said energy is never destroyed. So where does most of a gas car's fuel energy go? → **It is lost as heat, mainly in the engine**
  - L71 `question.everyday_technology.071.q3`: Level 2 said energy is never destroyed. So why does an open fridge door warm a kitchen instead of cooling it? → **Heat circles back out, and the running motor adds more**
  - L100 `question.everyday_technology.100.q2`: Why must a power-station generator be spun by steam, water, wind or gas? → **Energy can't be created, so its electricity must come from the motion it's given**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Physiology references give muscle efficiency of about 20 to 25% during exercise, with 75 to 80% released as heat; EIA says the body is under 5% efficient most of the time. Sources: https://phys.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Conceptual_Physics/Body_Physics_-_Motion_to_Metabolism_(Davis)/10:_Powering_the_Body/10.09:_Efficiency_of_the_Human_Body, https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/what-is-energy/laws-of-energy.php

  - L83 “Bridges” · `card.everyday_technology.083.c3` (text): Arch and suspension: push or hang / An arch carries its load mainly by compression. Once you see squeeze and stretch, every bridge and building becomes a puzzle you can read.

  - L10 “Checkpoint: Energy and Electricity” · `card.everyday_technology.010.c2` (comparison): Electricity: made, stored, used: Made (Generators spin a magnet inside coils (Level 8); Turbines turn most of them) vs Stored (Batteries hold chemical energy (Level 6); Recharging runs the reaction backward) vs Used (Bulbs turn it into light and heat (Level 5); Motors turn it into motion (Level 7))

Level 6's rule still applies: charging drives current through the battery in reverse, running the reaction backward to store energy again. The chips that run it all get their own chapter.

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.telephone_how`: unverified

> **Claim:** A telephone's transmitter turns the vibrations of a diaphragm into a current that varies like the sound wave (an analogue signal); at the receiver the changing current in an electromagnet vibrates another diaphragm, recreating the sound.

- **Concept:** How a telephone carries a voice (`concept.everyday_technology.telephone_voice_current`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L43 “The Telephone” · `card.everyday_technology.043.c2` (text): A current shaped like your voice / Level 42's telegraph only switched current on and off. A telephone does something subtler. Your voice makes a thin diaphragm vibrate, and the transmitter turns those vibrations into a current that rises and falls like the sound wave itself. At the other end, the changing current drives an electromagnet that shakes a second diaphragm, rebuilding the sound. The wire carries a copy of your voice, drawn in electricity.
  - L50 “Milestone: Energy to Information” · `card.everyday_technology.050.c3` (text): Same electricity, two jobs / Power is about how much energy flows. A signal is about the pattern. The telegraph's pattern was on and off: dots and dashes. The telephone's was a current that rose and fell like a sound wave. Radio sent patterns through the air as waves, and television sent the brightness of each spot. A tiny current can carry a big message, because what matters is its shape.
  - L50 “Milestone: Energy to Information” · `card.everyday_technology.050.c4` (comparison): Chapter 1 is hiding inside Chapter 5: Electromagnets (Level 7) (Mark dots at the telegraph's far end; Shake telephone earpieces and phone speakers) vs Batteries (Level 6) (Power the phone in your pocket; Recharge by running the reaction backward) vs Changing currents (Levels 8-9) (Bell's telephone idea relied on induction; A changing current in an antenna sends out radio waves)
- **Tested by:**

  - L45 `question.everyday_technology.045.q3`: A telephone turns sound into a rising and falling current. What does a TV camera turn into a rising and falling signal? → **The brightness of each spot it scans**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. TechnologyUK: the voltage waveform on an analogue telephone line is an analogue of the speaker's sound waves; the Smithsonian's description of Bell's experimental telephone has a diaphragm with a metal plate facing an electromagnet at each end. ### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.ampere_electrons`: unverified

> **Claim:** One ampere is a flow of one coulomb of charge per second, about 6.2 billion billion (6.2 x 10^18) electrons per second.

- **Concept:** Electric current (`concept.everyday_technology.electric_current`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L3 “Electricity” · `card.everyday_technology.003.c3` (fact): Current counts how many electrons pass, not how fast they go. / Current is measured in amperes. One ampere means about 6.2 billion billion electrons passing a point every second. Each one is slow, but there are so many that the flow adds up. And when you close a switch, the push reaches every electron in the circuit at nearly the speed of light, so they all start moving at once. The light doesn't wait.
  - L3 “Electricity” · `card.everyday_technology.003.c4` (text): Voltage is the push / Voltage says how much energy each bit of charge gets. One volt means one joule for every coulomb, the charge one ampere carries in a second. An analogy helps, if you remember it's only a picture: a battery is like the pump that lifts water to the top of a water slide, so it can run back down. A 1.5-volt battery gives each coulomb 1.5 joules for the trip around.
- **Tested by:**
  - L3 `question.everyday_technology.003.q2`: Electrons drift slowly, so why does a lamp light the instant you flip the switch? → **The push reaches every electron almost at once**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. OpenStax: 1 A = 1 C/s. With NIST's exact elementary charge 1.602176634 x 10^-19 C, one coulomb is 6.24 x 10^18 electrons. Sources: https://openstax.org/books/college-physics-2e/pages/20-1-current, https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.330-2019.pdf

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.induction_needs_change`: unverified

> **Claim:** Induction needs a changing magnetic field: a steady field through a coil induces nothing, and the faster the field changes, the larger the voltage.

- **Concept:** Electromagnetic induction (`concept.everyday_technology.electromagnetic_induction`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L8 “Generators” · `card.everyday_technology.008.c2` (text): Faraday's discovery: change makes current / In 1831, Michael Faraday found that moving a magnet inside a coil of wire makes a current flow in the wire. The key word is moving. A magnet sitting still inside a coil does nothing. What counts is a changing magnetic field, and the faster it changes, the bigger the voltage. This is called electromagnetic induction.
  - L38 “Traffic” · `card.everyday_technology.038.c3` (text): How the light knows you're waiting / Near many traffic lights, a loop of wire is sawn into the road. It's the most common signal sensor. An electronics unit energizes the loop with a current that keeps changing, and Level 8 showed that a changing magnetic field induces current. Park over the loop, and currents flow in your car's metal, lowering the loop's inductance. The unit reads that as a car and calls for a green.
- **Tested by:**
  - L8 `question.everyday_technology.008.q2`: A strong magnet sits perfectly still inside a coil of wire. What happens? → **No current flows**
  - L9 `question.everyday_technology.009.q3`: Transformers work by Level 8's induction. Why does that mean they need AC? → **Induction needs a magnetic field that keeps changing**
  - L38 `question.everyday_technology.038.q3`: A road loop senses your car because currents flow in the car's metal. Which Level 8 idea makes that happen? → **A changing magnetic field induces current**
  - L43 `question.everyday_technology.043.q3`: Bell reasoned that a vibrating membrane could induce a voltage in a coil. Which Level 8 discovery was he relying on? → **A changing magnetic field makes a current flow**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Physics references: a constant magnetic field (as from DC) induces no current in a stationary coil; induced voltage grows with the rate of change. ### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.electromagnet`: unverified

> **Claim:** An electromagnet is a coil of wire around a magnetic core such as iron; its magnetism can be switched on and off, strengthened or reversed by changing the current.

- **Concept:** Electricity makes magnetism (`concept.everyday_technology.electromagnetism`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L7 “Magnets and Motors” · `card.everyday_technology.007.c2` (text): Current makes a magnet / Every magnet has a north and a south pole. Opposite poles attract and like poles push apart, much like Level 3's charges. Ørsted's needle moved because a current makes its own magnetic field. Wind wire into a coil around an iron core and you get an electromagnet: a magnet you can switch on and off, strengthen or flip, just by changing the current.
  - L42 “The Telegraph” · `card.everyday_technology.042.c2` (text): A switch at one end, a magnet at the other / A telegraph is Level 4's circuit stretched between cities. The sender's key is a switch: press it and the loop closes, so current flows; let go and it opens. At the far end, that current switches an electromagnet on and off, just like the ones in Level 7. In Morse's system the magnet pulled a stylus that marked a moving strip of paper. A short signal made a dot, a longer one a dash.
- **Tested by:**
  - L7 `question.everyday_technology.007.q3`: Magnetic poles behave much like Level 3's electric charges. In what way? → **Opposites attract and likes push apart**
  - L42 `question.everyday_technology.042.q3`: Which Level 7 device, switched on and off by the incoming current, made the marks at a telegraph's receiving end? → **An electromagnet**
  - L50 `question.everyday_technology.050.q5`: Energy to information: which Chapter 1 idea is at work in both a telegraph receiver and a smartphone speaker? → **A current making a magnetic field**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. LibreTexts Physical Science: an electromagnet's field exists only while current flows and disappears when it is turned off. Sources: https://phys.libretexts.org/Courses/Coalinga_College/Physical_Science_for_Educators_(CID:_PHYS_14)/12:_Magnetism/12.05:_Electromagnetism/12.5.01:_Electromagnet

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.energy_conservation`: unverified

> **Claim:** Energy is neither created nor destroyed; when it is used it changes from one form into another.

- **Concept:** Energy changes form (`concept.everyday_technology.energy_conservation`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L2 “What Energy Is” · `card.everyday_technology.002.c1` (text): Nobody has ever made a single joule of energy. / Not power stations, not batteries, not your breakfast. Energy can't be created. Everything that seems to make it is really changing it from one form into another. To see how, start with what energy actually is.
  - L2 “What Energy Is” · `card.everyday_technology.002.c3` (text): Energy never vanishes. It changes jobs. / Energy can't be created or destroyed, only changed from one form into another. Your breakfast holds chemical energy, and your body turns it into motion when you walk or play. But even at its best, your body turns only about a quarter of that energy into motion, and most of the rest becomes heat. That's why exercise warms you up. Nothing was lost; it just changed form.
  - L5 “The Light Bulb” · `card.everyday_technology.005.c4` (text): LEDs: light without the hot wire / An LED (light-emitting diode) has no filament. It's made of two semiconductor materials, and when current crosses the junction between them, electrons give up energy directly as light. The material sets the color. Level 2's rule still holds: energy isn't destroyed, so less wasted as heat means more light per joule. LEDs use at least 75% less energy than incandescent bulbs and last many times longer.
  - L8 “Generators” · `card.everyday_technology.008.c4` (fact): A motor and a generator are the same machine, facing opposite ways. / A motor turns electrical energy into motion. A generator turns motion into electrical energy. Level 2's rule explains why a generator never gives something for nothing: energy can't be created, so every joule of electricity it makes started as the energy of whatever spun it.
  - L12 “Coal and Gas Plants” · `card.everyday_technology.012.c2` (text): Fire, water, steam, spin / In a coal plant, fuel burns in a boiler and heats water into steam. The steam pushes on blades attached to a shaft and spins the turbine. The turbine turns a generator: Level 8's spinning electromagnet inside coils of wire. Follow the energy and it's Level 2's rule at work. Chemical energy in the fuel becomes heat, heat becomes motion, and motion becomes electricity.
  - L12 “Coal and Gas Plants” · `card.everyday_technology.012.c3` (fact): A coal plant turns only about a third of its fuel's energy into electricity. / That was the US average in 2024. The other two-thirds ends up as waste heat. Nothing is destroyed, as Level 2 promised; it just ends up somewhere useless. It's Level 5's old light bulb problem on a giant scale: most of the energy leaves as heat.
  - L18 “Storing Energy” · `card.everyday_technology.018.c2` (text): You can't bottle electricity / Grid storage keeps energy as something else: water pumped uphill, chemicals in batteries, heat, compressed air or a spinning flywheel. Then it turns it back into electricity. That round trip costs something: storage always uses more electricity to charge than it gives back. And it makes no energy of its own, which is Level 2's rule again. Its job is timing: moving power from when there's plenty to when there isn't.
  - L21 “Levers, Wheels and Pulleys” · `card.everyday_technology.021.c4` (fact): No machine gives you free work. / The extra force always costs distance. With 4 strands holding the load, you have to haul in 4 meters of rope to lift it 1 meter. Force times distance, the work, comes out the same, and friction takes a little extra on top. Level 2's rule again: energy is never created, not even by Archimedes.
  - L26 “Friction and Brakes” · `card.everyday_technology.026.c3` (text): Brakes turn motion into heat / A disc brake is friction on purpose. Pads press against a metal disc that turns with the wheel, and the rubbing slows it. Level 2's rule decides where the car's energy of motion goes: it can't vanish, so it becomes heat in the brakes. Rub your hands together fast and you can feel the same trick, just smaller.
  - L30 “Checkpoint: Engines and Motion” · `card.everyday_technology.030.c4` (text): One rule under all of them / No machine in this chapter makes energy. A gas engine turns fuel into motion but loses most of it as heat. An electric car loses far less, getting over 77% of its plug energy to the wheels. Levers, gears and hydraulics only reshape a push: more force, paid for with more distance. Horsepower and watts just measure how fast any of them delivers the energy.
  - L67 “The Cloud” · `card.everyday_technology.067.c4` (text): Where all that energy goes / Level 2's rule still holds: energy is never destroyed, it only changes form. In a data center, most of the electricity ends up as heat, and that heat has to be carried away before the machines overheat. Cooling alone can take up to 40% of a data center's energy. Your photo backup is, in a small way, a space heater.
  - L71 “Refrigerators” · `card.everyday_technology.071.c4` (fact): An open fridge door heats your kitchen. / Level 2's rule explains it: energy is never destroyed, only changed from one form to another. With the door open, heat just circles from the room into the fridge and straight back out. Meanwhile the motor keeps running, and it adds heat of its own. The result is a warmer kitchen and a fridge working hard for nothing.
  - L75 “Heating and Cooling” · `card.everyday_technology.075.c4` (fact): A heat pump can move about 3 kWh of heat indoors using 1 kWh of electricity. / An ordinary electric heater turns each kilowatt-hour, Level 10's unit, into one kilowatt-hour of heat. A heat pump spends its electricity moving heat that already exists, so it can bring in about three. Level 2's rule survives: nothing is created, just transferred. That's why heat pumps are so much more efficient than traditional heating.

  - L12 `question.everyday_technology.012.q3`: A coal plant turns only about a third of its fuel's energy into electricity. Where does the rest go? → **It ends up as waste heat**

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.motion_gear_teeth_speed`: unverified

> **Claim:** Gears pass rotation through meshing teeth without slipping; a driven gear with twice as many teeth as the gear driving it turns at half the speed, with twice the torque.

- **Concept:** Gear ratios (`concept.everyday_technology.motion_gear_ratio`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L27 “Gears” · `card.everyday_technology.027.c2` (text): Teeth set the ratio / A gear is a wheel with teeth. When two gears mesh, the teeth can't slip, so both gears pass the same number of teeth every second. Give the driven gear twice as many teeth as the one driving it, and it turns at half the speed. Count the teeth and you know the ratio.
  - L27 “Gears” · `card.everyday_technology.027.c3` (text): Slower, but stronger / That slower gear also turns with twice the twisting force, called torque. It's Level 21's wheel and axle again: gears multiply force by the ratio of their sizes, like levers that go round. Flip the pair, with a big gear driving a small one, and you get speed instead of force. Either way, Level 21's rule holds: no gear hands out free energy.
- **Tested by:**
  - L27 `question.everyday_technology.027.q1`: A gear with 10 teeth drives a gear with 20 teeth. How fast does the bigger gear turn? → **Half as fast**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. OpenStax (Simple Machines) gives gears the same ratio-of-radii mechanical advantage; Wikipedia (Gear train) gives speed ratio from tooth counts. Sources: https://openstax.org/books/college-physics-2e/pages/9-5-simple-machines, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gear_train

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.internet_cerf_kahn_tcp`: unverified

> **Claim:** In 1974 Vinton Cerf and Robert Kahn published TCP, a design for joining separately built packet networks (including radio and satellite ones) into one network of networks.

In 1974, Vinton Cerf and Robert Kahn published TCP, a design for joining separately built networks, even radio and satellite ones, into one network of networks. On January 1, 1983, ARPANET switched to TCP/IP, with every connected computer converting at the same time. That shared set of rules is what makes the internet one thing. It isn't a single machine. It's an agreement.
  - L65 “The Web” · `card.everyday_technology.065.c2` (text): Roads and deliveries / The internet is the infrastructure: a huge network of computers talking to each other, the network of networks from Level 61. The web is one service built on top of it. It isn't the only one: email is another. Picture the internet as the road system and the web as one kind of traffic on it. Send an email with no browser open, and you've used the internet without touching the web.

> **Claim:** An LED (light-emitting diode) is a semiconductor device with no filament: when current crosses the junction between two semiconductor materials, electrons release energy as light, and the material sets the color.

  - L5 “The Light Bulb” · `card.everyday_technology.005.c4` (text): LEDs: light without the hot wire / An LED (light-emitting diode) has no filament. It's made of two semiconductor materials, and when current crosses the junction between them, electrons give up energy directly as light. The material sets the color. Level 2's rule still holds: energy isn't destroyed, so less wasted as heat means more light per joule. LEDs use at least 75% less energy than incandescent bulbs and last many times longer.
  - L17 “Solar Power” · `card.everyday_technology.017.c2` (text): Light knocks electrons loose / A solar cell, or photovoltaic (PV) cell, is made of a semiconductor, like Level 5's LED. When it absorbs enough sunlight, electrons are knocked loose and move toward the cell's front surface. That builds up a charge imbalance, like the two ends of a battery. Connect the cell into a circuit and current flows. An LED turns electricity into light; a solar cell runs the trick the other way.
  - L47 “How a Screen Works” · `card.everyday_technology.047.c4` (text): An LCD is a wall of tiny shutters / An LCD makes no light of its own. > **Claim:** Stations put sound on a radio-frequency carrier wave: AM varies the carrier's amplitude (strength) to match the sound, while FM keeps the amplitude constant and varies the frequency.

- **Appears in:**
  - L44 “Radio” · `card.everyday_technology.044.c3` (text): Riding the wave: AM and FM / A station sends out a carrier wave at its own frequency, and tuning your radio picks that frequency out. To carry sound, the station changes the wave. AM (amplitude modulation) varies the wave's strength to match the sound. FM (frequency modulation) keeps the strength steady and varies the frequency instead. Your radio reads the changes and drives its speaker. It's Level 43's voice-shaped signal, sent through the air.
  - L50 “Milestone: Energy to Information” · `card.everyday_technology.050.c3` (text): Same electricity, two jobs / Power is about how much energy flows. A signal is about the pattern. The telegraph's pattern was on and off: dots and dashes. The telephone's was a current that rose and fell like a sound wave. Radio sent patterns through the air as waves, and television sent the brightness of each spot. A tiny current can carry a big message, because what matters is its shape.
- **Tested by:**
  - L44 `question.everyday_technology.044.q2`: How does an FM station put sound onto its carrier wave? → **By varying the wave's frequency to match the sound**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. PBS (A Science Odyssey) and ScienceABC explain that AM varies the height (amplitude) of the carrier and FM varies its frequency while the amplitude stays constant. ### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.motion_hydraulic_force`: unverified

> **Claim:** In a hydraulic system the pressure is the same on both pistons, so a piston with 10 times the area pushes with 10 times the force (F1/A1 = F2/A2).

- **Appears in:**

Connect a small piston to one with 10 times the area: the pressure on both is the same, so the big piston pushes with 10 times the force. The catch is Level 21's rule. To raise the big piston 1 centimeter, the small one must travel 10. Force up, distance up, energy the same.

- **Tested by:**

  - L30 `question.everyday_technology.030.q4`: Engines and Motion recap: what do a pulley system, a pair of gears and a hydraulic lift have in common? → **They multiply force but cost extra distance**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Britannica and OpenStax give the same area-ratio force multiplication. Sources: https://www.britannica.com/science/Pascals-principle

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.penicillin_cell_wall`: unverified

> **Claim:** Penicillin stops bacteria from building their cell walls, leaving them leaky and fragile so they burst; human cells have no such walls.

Without a sturdy wall, a bacterium turns leaky and fragile, and it bursts. Your own cells have no such wall, so the drug leaves them alone. That's the trick of an antibiotic: hit something bacteria have and you don't. Viruses, like those behind colds and flu, lack those targets, so antibiotics don't work on them.

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. University of Hawaii: penicillin inhibits peptidoglycan, making cells leaky and fragile so they burst; human cells lack peptidoglycan. ### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.computer_four_jobs`: unverified

> **Claim:** A computer has input devices such as a keyboard or mouse, a central processing unit (CPU) that processes data, memory that holds data and instructions, and output devices such as a screen or printer.

- **Appears in:**
  - L51 “What a Computer Is” · `card.everyday_technology.051.c3` (text): Four jobs: in, process, remember, out / Every computer does four jobs. Input brings information in: a key press, a mouse click. Processing works on it, in the central processing unit, or CPU. Memory holds the data and the instructions while the work happens. Output sends the result back out, as letters on a screen or a page from the printer. Type a single letter and all four jobs take part.
  - L51 “What a Computer Is” · `card.everyday_technology.051.c4` (text): The human computer did all four / Picture a Langley computer at her desk. Wind-tunnel readings arrive: input. She works through the arithmetic: processing. Her notes hold the numbers in between: memory. A plotted result goes to the engineers: output. When electronic computers arrived, many of these women took on programming them. The machine didn't invent a new job. It took over a human one, and kept the job title.
  - L60 “Checkpoint: Computers” · `card.everyday_technology.060.c2` (text): One key press, start to finish / The key press is input (Level 51). The letter becomes a byte: lowercase a is 01100001 in ASCII (Level 52). It lands in RAM (Level 54), where your app, running under the operating system, works on it. The processor's billions of transistor switches (Level 53) do the processing. The result goes out as colored pixels on your screen: output.
- **Tested by:**

  - L57 `question.everyday_technology.057.q3`: Babbage's Analytical Engine had a "store" and a "mill". Which of Level 51's four computer jobs did the mill do? → **Processing**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Britannica on the personal computer lists a CPU, memory and peripherals such as display, keyboard, mouse and printer; the CPU entry describes processing and main memory. > **Claim:** Television sends a picture by scanning it spot by spot, left to right along a line and then one line lower, turning each spot's brightness into an electrical signal; the receiver rebuilds it in the same order, fast enough for the eye to see a whole picture.

A TV camera scans the scene like a reader: start at the top left, sweep right, jump back one line lower, repeat. Each spot's brightness becomes part of an electrical signal. The telegraph's pattern was on and off: dots and dashes. The telephone's was a current that rose and fell like a sound wave. ### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.echo_radar_ranging`: unverified

> **Claim:** Radar (radio detection and ranging) sends radio pulses and finds distance from the round-trip time of the echo, out to the target and back.

- **Concept:** Radar (`concept.everyday_technology.echo_radar`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L35 “Radar and Sonar” · `card.everyday_technology.035.c2` (text): Radar: shout, listen, time it / Radar stands for radio detection and ranging. It sends out pulses of radio waves and listens for echoes. Distance comes from timing the round trip, out to the target and back, then halving it. Radio waves travel at the speed of light, about 300,000 km every second, so an echo from a plane 150 km away comes back in about a thousandth of a second.
  - L39 “Self-Driving Cars” · `card.everyday_technology.039.c2` (text): Seeing with timers / A self-driving car carries cameras, radar and lidar, plus GPS and highly detailed maps of its roads. Radar works just like Level 35's: time the radio echo. Lidar does the same with pulses of laser light, measuring the distance to whatever each pulse bounces off. Computers fuse it all into a 3-D map of the surroundings and keep adjusting steering, speed and braking.
  - L40 “Checkpoint: Getting Around” · `card.everyday_technology.040.c4` (text): Finding the way: time a wave / The chapter's other trick is a stopwatch. Radar times a radio echo's round trip and halves it. Sonar does the same with sound, which crosses seawater at about 1,500 meters a second. GPS times one-way signals instead, which only works because the satellites carry atomic clocks, corrected for relativity. Distance is speed times time, whether you're a ship, a plane or a phone.
- **Tested by:**
  - L35 `question.everyday_technology.035.q1`: How does radar work out how far away an airplane is? → **It times how long a radio echo takes to return**
  - L37 `question.everyday_technology.037.q3`: Level 35's radar times an echo that goes out and back. How is GPS timing different? → **GPS measures a one-way trip the receiver only hears**
  - L39 `question.everyday_technology.039.q3`: Level 35's radar and a self-driving car's lidar both measure distance. How? → **By timing how long a pulse takes to bounce back**
  - L40 `question.everyday_technology.040.q5`: Getting Around recap: radar halves its echo time, but GPS does not. Why not? → **A GPS signal only travels one way**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Britannica "Radar: Pulse radar" and Wikipedia: range equals cT/2, where T is the round-trip time; radar is an acronym for radio detection and ranging. Sources: https://www.britannica.com/technology/radar/Pulse-radar

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.build_reinforced_concrete`: unverified

> **Claim:** Plain concrete handles compression but not tension, which makes it unsuitable for most structures on its own; reinforced concrete embeds steel, whose tensile strength works with concrete's compressive strength.

- **Concept:** Concrete and reinforced concrete (`concept.everyday_technology.build_concrete_basics`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L84 “Concrete” · `card.everyday_technology.084.c3` (text): Strong when squeezed, weak when stretched / Remember Level 83's beam: squeezed on top, stretched underneath. Plain concrete handles squeezing well but copes badly with stretching, which makes it unsuitable for most structures on its own. The fix is reinforced concrete: steel bars cast inside. The steel takes the tension, the concrete takes the compression, and together they can span gaps neither could manage alone.
  - L86 “Steel” · `card.everyday_technology.086.c2` (text): Steel is iron with a pinch of carbon / Pure iron is soft. Add carbon and it gets much harder: steel is iron with up to about 2 percent carbon. Keep going, to 2 to 4 percent, and you get cast iron, which holds up fine when squeezed but is brittle and weak when pulled. Level 83's tension is cast iron's weak spot. Steel handles pulling well, which is why it goes inside reinforced concrete.
  - L90 “Checkpoint: Building and Making” · `card.everyday_technology.090.c3` (comparison): Building and Making, in three columns: Materials (Steel: iron with up to about 2 percent carbon (Level 86); Concrete takes the squeeze; steel bars take the stretch (Level 84)) vs Building machines (Safe elevators made tall buildings practical (Level 82); TBMs dig and line tunnels with concrete rings (Level 85)) vs Making machines (Assembly lines split work into small repeated tasks (Level 87); Robots repeat taught moves; 3D printers add layers (Levels 88–89))
  - L90 “Checkpoint: Building and Making” · `card.everyday_technology.090.c4` (fact): Two forces run through the whole chapter: tension and compression. / An arch pushes its load into its supports; a suspension bridge hangs from cables in tension (Level 83). Concrete takes the squeeze while steel bars take the stretch (Level 84). Brittle cast iron is weak when pulled; steel is not (Level 86). Once you see squeeze and stretch, every bridge and building becomes a puzzle you can read.
- **Tested by:**

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.echo_sound_seawater`: unverified

> **Claim:** Sound travels through seawater at about 1,500 meters per second, so an echo after 2 seconds has gone 3,000 meters round trip: a 1,500-meter depth.

Hear the seafloor's echo 2 seconds after the ping, and the sound has gone 3,000 meters round trip: the bottom is 1,500 meters down.

> **Claim:** A lever turns on a pivot (fulcrum); force times distance from the fulcrum balances on each side, so an effort five times farther out than the load is multiplied five times.

Beating a world champion at chess counts. The name is older than most people guess: John McCarthy coined "artificial intelligence" in 1955. And by Level 1's definition, AI is plain technology: knowledge put to work on a practical job. The job just happens to look like thinking.

  - L51 `question.everyday_technology.051.q3`: Level 1 called technology knowledge put to work. How does a programmable computer fit that idea? → **It follows instructions you can swap to do new jobs**

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.telegraph_how`: unverified

> **Claim:** In Morse's telegraph a key made and broke the circuit; at the receiver an electromagnet, switched on and off by the signals, moved a stylus that marked dots (short signals) and dashes (longer ones) on moving paper.

- **Concept:** The electric telegraph (`concept.everyday_technology.telegraph_pulses`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L42 “The Telegraph” · `card.everyday_technology.042.c2` (text): A switch at one end, a magnet at the other / A telegraph is Level 4's circuit stretched between cities. The sender's key is a switch: press it and the loop closes, so current flows; let go and it opens. At the far end, that current switches an electromagnet on and off, just like the ones in Level 7. In Morse's system the magnet pulled a stylus that marked a moving strip of paper. A short signal made a dot, a longer one a dash.
  - L43 “The Telephone” · `card.everyday_technology.043.c2` (text): A current shaped like your voice / Level 42's telegraph only switched current on and off. A telephone does something subtler. Your voice makes a thin diaphragm vibrate, and the transmitter turns those vibrations into a current that rises and falls like the sound wave itself. At the other end, the changing current drives an electromagnet that shakes a second diaphragm, rebuilding the sound. The wire carries a copy of your voice, drawn in electricity.
  - L50 “Milestone: Energy to Information” · `card.everyday_technology.050.c3` (text): Same electricity, two jobs / Power is about how much energy flows. A signal is about the pattern. The telegraph's pattern was on and off: dots and dashes. The telephone's was a current that rose and fell like a sound wave. Radio sent patterns through the air as waves, and television sent the brightness of each spot. A tiny current can carry a big message, because what matters is its shape.
  - L50 “Milestone: Energy to Information” · `card.everyday_technology.050.c4` (comparison): Chapter 1 is hiding inside Chapter 5: Electromagnets (Level 7) (Mark dots at the telegraph's far end; Shake telephone earpieces and phone speakers) vs Batteries (Level 6) (Power the phone in your pocket; Recharge by running the reaction backward) vs Changing currents (Levels 8-9) (Bell's telephone idea relied on induction; A changing current in an antenna sends out radio waves)
- **Tested by:**
  - L42 `question.everyday_technology.042.q1`: In Morse's telegraph, what happened when the operator pressed the sending key? → **It closed the circuit, so current flowed down the line**
  - L42 `question.everyday_technology.042.q3`: Which Level 7 device, switched on and off by the incoming current, made the marks at a telegraph's receiving end? → **An electromagnet**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. TechnologyUK: Morse's design used an electromagnet that moved a pen to mark a moving paper strip whenever current passed; HistoryNet: Vail's sending key was a sprung lever over a contact on the transmission wire. Sources: https://www.technologyuk.net/telecommunications/telecom-principles/analogue-and-digital-signals.shtml, https://historynet.com/morses-partner-argued-he-invented-famous-code-to-no-a-vail/

  - L8 “Generators” · `card.everyday_technology.008.c1` (text): Run a motor backwards and it makes electricity. / Level 7 turned current into motion. Now force the shaft to turn instead, so the coil spins between the magnets, and current comes out. The same machine can work either way, and spinning generators make most of the world's electricity.
  - L8 “Generators” · `card.everyday_technology.008.c4` (fact): A motor and a generator are the same machine, facing opposite ways. / A motor turns electrical energy into motion. A generator turns motion into electrical energy. Level 2's rule explains why a generator never gives something for nothing: energy can't be created, so every joule of electricity it makes started as the energy of whatever spun it.
  - L25 “Electric Cars” · `card.everyday_technology.025.c4` (text): Braking that charges the battery / Here's the clever part. When an electric car slows down, the turning wheels spin its motor, and the motor runs as a generator, just as Level 8 said a motor run backwards would. It makes electricity that goes back into the battery, and doing that work helps slow the car. This is regenerative braking: energy that braking would normally waste gets saved.

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.computer_chip_growth`: unverified

> **Claim:** From the 4004's 2,300 transistors (1971) to the M1's 16 billion (2020) is a rise of about 7 million times: almost 23 doublings in 49 years, about one every two years.

From 2,300 to 16 billion is almost 23 doublings in 49 years, about one every two years.

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.ac_60_hertz`: unverified

> **Claim:** US grid AC runs at 60 hertz, 60 complete back-and-forth cycles per second; most grids use 50 or 60.

- **Concept:** AC and DC (`concept.everyday_technology.alternating_current`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L9 “Edison, Tesla and AC” · `card.everyday_technology.009.c2` (text): DC flows one way. AC swings back and forth. / Direct current (DC) flows steadily in one direction, like the current from a battery. Alternating current (AC) keeps reversing. On the US grid it goes through 60 complete back-and-forth cycles every second: 60 hertz. Level 8's generators make that swing naturally. A two-pole generator making 60-hertz power spins 3,600 times a minute: 60 turns a second, one cycle per turn.
  - L60 “Checkpoint: Computers” · `card.everyday_technology.060.c4` (fact): A 3.2 GHz processor's clock ticks 3.2 billion times a second. / Clock speed counts those cycles in gigahertz: billions per second. Remember Level 9's grid, swinging back and forth 60 times a second? In one of those swings, that clock ticks about 53 million times. Speed isn't everything, though: the chip's design matters too.
  - L64 “Wi-Fi” · `card.everyday_technology.064.c3` (text): Two bands: reach or speed / Most routers offer two bands. The 2.4 GHz band reaches farther and gets through walls better. The 5 GHz band is faster but covers a shorter range. A hertz is one cycle per second, and giga means billion, so 2.4 GHz waves swing back and forth 2.4 billion times a second. Remember Level 9's 60-hertz AC? Wi-Fi swings 40 million times faster.
  - L72 “Microwave Ovens” · `card.everyday_technology.072.c2` (text): Twisting water, billions of times a second / The magnetron fills the oven with microwaves at about 2,450 megahertz. Water molecules in food have a slightly negative oxygen end and a slightly positive hydrogen end, and like Level 3's charges, those ends get pushed and pulled. The waves' field flips about 2.45 billion times a second, twisting the molecules back and forth until they jostle their neighbors. That jostling is heat. Level 9's grid current flips 60 times a second. Microwaves are busier.

> **Claim:** Energy is potential (stored), such as chemical energy in food and batteries, gravitational energy in raised objects and energy in stretched rubber bands, or kinetic (working): motion, heat, light, sound and electricity.

Stored (potential) energy waits: chemical energy in food and batteries, gravitational energy in anything lifted high, the energy in a stretched rubber band. Working (kinetic) energy is busy: motion, heat, light, sound and electricity. A sandwich and a raised hammer have something in common. Both are jobs waiting to happen.
  - L15 “Hydropower” · `card.everyday_technology.015.c2` (text): How a dam makes electricity / A dam holds back a reservoir of water. Near the bottom of the dam, water enters an intake and falls through a pipe called a penstock. At the end it spins a turbine, and the turbine's shaft turns a generator. No fire, no steam: the water pushes the turbine itself. It's Level 2's gravitational energy, the energy stored in anything raised high, cashed in.
  - L18 “Storing Energy” · `card.everyday_technology.018.c3` (text): The water battery / Pumped-storage hydropower uses spare electricity to run its turbines in reverse, pumping water up to a reservoir. Level 2 said anything lifted high stores gravitational energy; here the two ends mostly trade it back and forth.

Coal still made about a third on its own. And almost every source still ends the same way: something spins a turbine, and the turbine spins Level 8's generator. Solar panels are the big exception, with nothing spinning at all.
  - L32 “Jet Engines” · `card.everyday_technology.032.c3` (text): Inside: squeeze, burn, spin, blow / Air enters the front and meets the compressor, rows of spinning blades that raise its pressure. In the burner, fuel mixes with that air and burns. The hot gas rushes through a turbine and spins it, and a shaft carries that spin forward to drive the compressor. Then the nozzle shoots the gas out, faster than it came in. The turbine is a cousin of Level 8's: power stations spin theirs with burning gas too.

> **Claim:** At best the human body turns only about a quarter of its food energy into motion; most becomes heat, and most of the time the useful share is far lower.

Your breakfast holds chemical energy, and your body turns it into motion when you walk or play. But even at its best, your body turns only about a quarter of that energy into motion, and most of the rest becomes heat. That's why exercise warms you up. Nothing was lost; it just changed form.

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.energy_conservation`: unverified

> **Claim:** Energy is neither created nor destroyed; when it is used it changes from one form into another.

- **Concept:** Energy changes form (`concept.everyday_technology.energy_conservation`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L2 “What Energy Is” · `card.everyday_technology.002.c1` (text): Nobody has ever made a single joule of energy. / Not power stations, not batteries, not your breakfast. Energy can't be created. Everything that seems to make it is really changing it from one form into another. To see how, start with what energy actually is.
  - L2 “What Energy Is” · `card.everyday_technology.002.c3` (text): Energy never vanishes. It changes jobs. / Energy can't be created or destroyed, only changed from one form into another. Your breakfast holds chemical energy, and your body turns it into motion when you walk or play. But even at its best, your body turns only about a quarter of that energy into motion, and most of the rest becomes heat. That's why exercise warms you up. Nothing was lost; it just changed form.
  - L5 “The Light Bulb” · `card.everyday_technology.005.c4` (text): LEDs: light without the hot wire / An LED (light-emitting diode) has no filament. It's made of two semiconductor materials, and when current crosses the junction between them, electrons give up energy directly as light. The material sets the color. Level 2's rule still holds: energy isn't destroyed, so less wasted as heat means more light per joule. LEDs use at least 75% less energy than incandescent bulbs and last many times longer.
  - L8 “Generators” · `card.everyday_technology.008.c4` (fact): A motor and a generator are the same machine, facing opposite ways. / A motor turns electrical energy into motion. A generator turns motion into electrical energy. Level 2's rule explains why a generator never gives something for nothing: energy can't be created, so every joule of electricity it makes started as the energy of whatever spun it.
  - L12 “Coal and Gas Plants” · `card.everyday_technology.012.c2` (text): Fire, water, steam, spin / In a coal plant, fuel burns in a boiler and heats water into steam. The steam pushes on blades attached to a shaft and spins the turbine. The turbine turns a generator: Level 8's spinning electromagnet inside coils of wire. Follow the energy and it's Level 2's rule at work. Chemical energy in the fuel becomes heat, heat becomes motion, and motion becomes electricity.
  - L12 “Coal and Gas Plants” · `card.everyday_technology.012.c3` (fact): A coal plant turns only about a third of its fuel's energy into electricity. / That was the US average in 2024. The other two-thirds ends up as waste heat. Nothing is destroyed, as Level 2 promised; it just ends up somewhere useless. It's Level 5's old light bulb problem on a giant scale: most of the energy leaves as heat.
  - L18 “Storing Energy” · `card.everyday_technology.018.c2` (text): You can't bottle electricity / Grid storage keeps energy as something else: water pumped uphill, chemicals in batteries, heat, compressed air or a spinning flywheel. Then it turns it back into electricity. That round trip costs something: storage always uses more electricity to charge than it gives back. And it makes no energy of its own, which is Level 2's rule again. Its job is timing: moving power from when there's plenty to when there isn't.
  - L21 “Levers, Wheels and Pulleys” · `card.everyday_technology.021.c4` (fact): No machine gives you free work. / The extra force always costs distance. With 4 strands holding the load, you have to haul in 4 meters of rope to lift it 1 meter. Force times distance, the work, comes out the same, and friction takes a little extra on top. Level 2's rule again: energy is never created, not even by Archimedes.
  - L26 “Friction and Brakes” · `card.everyday_technology.026.c3` (text): Brakes turn motion into heat / A disc brake is friction on purpose. Pads press against a metal disc that turns with the wheel, and the rubbing slows it. Level 2's rule decides where the car's energy of motion goes: it can't vanish, so it becomes heat in the brakes. Rub your hands together fast and you can feel the same trick, just smaller.
  - L30 “Checkpoint: Engines and Motion” · `card.everyday_technology.030.c4` (text): One rule under all of them / No machine in this chapter makes energy. A gas engine turns fuel into motion but loses most of it as heat. An electric car loses far less, getting over 77% of its plug energy to the wheels. Levers, gears and hydraulics only reshape a push: more force, paid for with more distance. Horsepower and watts just measure how fast any of them delivers the energy.
  - L67 “The Cloud” · `card.everyday_technology.067.c4` (text): Where all that energy goes / Level 2's rule still holds: energy is never destroyed, it only changes form. In a data center, most of the electricity ends up as heat, and that heat has to be carried away before the machines overheat. Cooling alone can take up to 40% of a data center's energy. Your photo backup is, in a small way, a space heater.
  - L71 “Refrigerators” · `card.everyday_technology.071.c4` (fact): An open fridge door heats your kitchen. / Level 2's rule explains it: energy is never destroyed, only changed from one form to another. With the door open, heat just circles from the room into the fridge and straight back out. Meanwhile the motor keeps running, and it adds heat of its own. The result is a warmer kitchen and a fridge working hard for nothing.
  - L75 “Heating and Cooling” · `card.everyday_technology.075.c4` (fact): A heat pump can move about 3 kWh of heat indoors using 1 kWh of electricity. / An ordinary electric heater turns each kilowatt-hour, Level 10's unit, into one kilowatt-hour of heat. A heat pump spends its electricity moving heat that already exists, so it can bring in about three. Level 2's rule survives: nothing is created, just transferred. That's why heat pumps are so much more efficient than traditional heating.

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.kilowatt_hour`: unverified

> **Claim:** A kilowatt-hour is 1,000 watts for one hour (3,600 seconds): 3.6 million joules.

- **Appears in:**
  - L10 “Checkpoint: Energy and Electricity” · `card.everyday_technology.010.c4` (fact): A kilowatt-hour is 3.6 million joules. / That's 1,000 watts running for an hour (3,600 seconds), and it's the unit utilities measure and charge for. In apples, that's 3.6 million small apples, each lifted a meter. Swap an old bulb for an LED, which uses at least 75% less energy, and the same light takes a quarter or less of the kilowatt-hours.
  - L67 “The Cloud” · `card.everyday_technology.067.c3` (fact): Data centers used about 415 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity in 2024. / That's the IEA's estimate of 415 terawatt-hours, around 1.5% of all the world's electricity. Each of those kilowatt-hours is Level 10's 3.6 million joules. Per unit of floor space, a data center uses 10 to 50 times the energy of a typical office building, says the US Department of Energy.
  - L75 “Heating and Cooling” · `card.everyday_technology.075.c4` (fact): A heat pump can move about 3 kWh of heat indoors using 1 kWh of electricity. / An ordinary electric heater turns each kilowatt-hour, Level 10's unit, into one kilowatt-hour of heat. A heat pump spends its electricity moving heat that already exists, so it can bring in about three. Level 2's rule survives: nothing is created, just transferred. That's why heat pumps are so much more efficient than traditional heating.

By Level 10's math, 3.15 megajoules is under one kilowatt-hour.
- **Tested by:**

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.charge_basics`: unverified

> **Claim:** Electrons carry negative charge and protons positive charge; opposite charges attract and like charges repel.

- **Concept:** Electric current (`concept.everyday_technology.electric_current`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L3 “Electricity” · `card.everyday_technology.003.c2` (text): Electricity is charge on the move / Atoms hold positive protons and negative electrons. Opposite charges attract; like charges push apart. In a metal wire, when electrons all drift the same way, that's an electric current. And those electrons were in the wire all along, belonging to its own atoms. A wire isn't an empty pipe waiting to be filled. It comes already full.
  - L7 “Magnets and Motors” · `card.everyday_technology.007.c2` (text): Current makes a magnet / Every magnet has a north and a south pole. Opposite poles attract and like poles push apart, much like Level 3's charges. Ørsted's needle moved because a current makes its own magnetic field. Wind wire into a coil around an iron core and you get an electromagnet: a magnet you can switch on and off, strengthen or flip, just by changing the current.
  - L72 “Microwave Ovens” · `card.everyday_technology.072.c2` (text): Twisting water, billions of times a second / The magnetron fills the oven with microwaves at about 2,450 megahertz. Water molecules in food have a slightly negative oxygen end and a slightly positive hydrogen end, and like Level 3's charges, those ends get pushed and pulled. The waves' field flips about 2.45 billion times a second, twisting the molecules back and forth until they jostle their neighbors. That jostling is heat. Level 9's grid current flips 60 times a second. Microwaves are busier.
  - L96 “Fusion Power” · `card.everyday_technology.096.c3` (text): Why it's so hard: nuclei don't want to touch / Remember Level 3: like charges repel. Nuclei are all positively charged, so they push each other away. To make them fuse, the fuel must be heated until the nuclei have enough energy to overcome that push. ITER says deuterium-tritium fusion needs 150,000,000 °C, 10 times hotter than the core of the Sun. At that heat the fuel is a plasma. Tokamaks hold it with magnetic fields; NIF squeezes its fuel with lasers.
- **Tested by:**
  - L3 `question.everyday_technology.003.q1`: What is an electric current? → **Charge moving through a wire**
  - L4 `question.everyday_technology.004.q3`: Level 3 said a wire is already full of electrons. So why won't a bulb light when there's a gap in the wire? → **Without a closed loop, the charge can't flow around**
  - L7 `question.everyday_technology.007.q3`: Magnetic poles behave much like Level 3's electric charges. In what way? → **Opposites attract and likes push apart**

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.internet_baran_rand`: unverified

> **Claim:** In the early 1960s Paul Baran at RAND worked on a US Air Force network that would not fail if one of its nodes was destroyed, routing messages along whichever path worked.

- **Appears in:**
  - L62 “Packets” · `card.everyday_technology.062.c3` (text): Designed to survive damage / Why chop things up at all? In the early 1960s, Paul Baran at the RAND Corporation worked on a US Air Force network that would not fail if one of its nodes was destroyed: messages would go along whichever path still worked. In Britain, Donald Davies at the National Physical Laboratory reached the same idea on his own, and in a 1966 proposal he named the pieces "packets."
  - L63 “Undersea Cables” · `card.everyday_technology.063.c3` (fact): Ships' anchors are a bigger threat to the internet than sharks. / Fishing vessels and dragged anchors cause about two-thirds of cable faults. Fish bites, sharks included, caused zero faults from 2007 to 2014, according to International Cable Protection Committee data. Breaks still happen, so countries use several cables and networks spread traffic across them. When one breaks, data keeps flowing over the others: Baran's idea from Level 62, a network that survives losing a piece.
- **Tested by:**
  - L62 `question.everyday_technology.062.q1`: Who gave internet data packets their name? → **Donald Davies**
  - L63 `question.everyday_technology.063.q3`: Networks spread their traffic across several undersea cables. Which Level 62 design goal does that echo? → **A network that keeps working when one piece is lost**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. ## Milestones: Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) Enables the Internet, 1974 (IEEE Engineering and Technology History Wiki)

- **Source:** `source.ethw_tcp_milestone`
- **URL:** https://ethw.org/Milestones:Transmission_Control_Protocol_(TCP)_Enables_the_Internet,_1974
- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.internet_cerf_kahn_tcp`: unverified

> **Claim:** In 1974 Vinton Cerf and Robert Kahn published TCP, a design for joining separately built packet networks (including radio and satellite ones) into one network of networks.

- **Concept:** TCP/IP: the network of networks (`concept.everyday_technology.internet_tcp_ip`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L61 “How the Internet Began” · `card.everyday_technology.061.c3` (text): A network of networks / ARPANET was only one network. In 1974, Vinton Cerf and Robert Kahn published TCP, a design for joining separately built networks, even radio and satellite ones, into one network of networks. On January 1, 1983, ARPANET switched to TCP/IP, with every connected computer converting at the same time. That shared set of rules is what makes the internet one thing. It isn't a single machine. It's an agreement.
  - L65 “The Web” · `card.everyday_technology.065.c2` (text): Roads and deliveries / The internet is the infrastructure: a huge network of computers talking to each other, the network of networks from Level 61. The web is one service built on top of it. It isn't the only one: email is another. Picture the internet as the road system and the web as one kind of traffic on it. Send an email with no browser open, and you've used the internet without touching the web.
- **Tested by:**
  - L61 `question.everyday_technology.061.q2`: Why is the internet called a "network of networks"? → **Shared TCP/IP rules let separate networks join as one**
  - L62 `question.everyday_technology.062.q3`: Level 61 introduced TCP/IP. What does TCP do when one of a message's packets goes missing? → **Spots the gap and has that packet sent again**
  - L65 `question.everyday_technology.065.q3`: How is the World Wide Web related to Level 61's "network of networks"? → **The web is one service that runs on top of it**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. The Cerf-Kahn paper "A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication" (IEEE Trans. Communications, May 1974) is reproduced by Princeton; the ACM Turing Award page credits Kahn and Cerf with TCP/IP internetworking. Sources: https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/fall06/cos561/papers/cerf74.pdf, https://amturing.acm.org/award_winners/kahn_4598637.cfm

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.build_counterweight`: unverified

> **Claim:** An elevator's counterweight weighs roughly as much as the car loaded half full, so the motor lifts only the difference in weight, plus a little extra to overcome friction.

- **Concept:** The elevator counterweight (`concept.everyday_technology.build_elevator_counterweight`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L82 “Elevators” · `card.everyday_technology.082.c3` (fact): An elevator's counterweight weighs about as much as the car half full. / Car and counterweight hang from the same cables, which run over a grooved wheel called a sheave that a motor turns. As the car goes up, the counterweight goes down. So the motor only lifts the difference in weight, plus a little to beat friction. Level 2 said anything lifted high stores gravitational energy; here the two ends mostly trade it back and forth.
- **Tested by:**
  - L82 `question.everyday_technology.082.q3`: Level 2 said anything lifted high stores gravitational energy. Why does an elevator's counterweight save the motor work? → **The motor only lifts the difference in weight**
  - L90 `question.everyday_technology.090.q2`: What do a tower crane's concrete counterweights have in common with Level 82's elevator counterweight? → **Both balance the load on the other side**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. HowStuffWorks: the counterweight equals the car plus about 40 percent of capacity, so the motor only has to overcome the difference; industry texts cite 40 to 50 percent balancing. Sources: https://science.howstuffworks.com/transport/engines-equipment/elevator3.htm

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.touch_how`: unverified

> **Claim:** On a capacitive touchscreen, your finger, which conducts electricity, alters an electric field by an amount that depends on where it is; these screens can sense several touches at once.

- **Appears in:**

The screen carries an electric field, and your finger, which conducts electricity, disturbs that field by an amount that depends on where it is. The phone works out the spot, and it can track several fingers at once. A plain plastic stylus does nothing, because plastic is an insulator, Level 4's word for a material that stops the flow of charge.
- **Tested by:**

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. ScienceAlert and TechTarget describe a conductive finger changing the charge or field at a point on a capacitive screen, which the phone locates. ## Cyber Actors Exploit 'Secure' Websites in Phishing Campaigns (FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center)

- **Source:** `source.fbi_ic3_https_phishing`
- **URL:** https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2019/PSA190610

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.account_padlock_phishing`: unverified

> **Claim:** Phishing sites increasingly use HTTPS certificates too, so the FBI warns not to trust a site just because it shows a padlock.

- **Concept:** How accounts get attacked (`concept.everyday_technology.account_attacks`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L69 “Passwords and Hacking” · `card.everyday_technology.069.c2` (text): Three common ways in / Phishing: a message with urgent language, a request for your details or a look-alike address such as amazan.com lures you to a fake page. A padlock doesn't prove a site is honest, the FBI warns; phishing sites use HTTPS too. Credential stuffing: username and password pairs leaked in one breach get tried on other sites. Guessing: attackers try common and previously leaked passwords first. None of these needs movie-style genius, just predictable habits.
- **Tested by:**
  - L69 `question.everyday_technology.069.q2`: Why is reusing one password on many sites risky? → **A leak at one site lets attackers into the others**
  - L69 `question.everyday_technology.069.q3`: A phishing page shows Level 68's padlock icon beside its address. What does the padlock actually tell you? → **Only that your traffic to it is encrypted**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Idwatchdog and PhishLabs report that most phishing sites now use HTTPS and repeat the FBI warning about the padlock. Sources: https://www.idwatchdog.com/education/-/article/reduce-risk-https-phishing, https://www.phishlabs.com/resources/press-releases/phishing-sites-trick-users-with-padlock-and-https

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.crypto_https_padlock`: unverified

> **Claim:** The "https" and padlock icon in a browser's address bar indicate that traffic to the site is encrypted.

- **Concept:** Public-key encryption (`concept.everyday_technology.crypto_public_key`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L68 “Encryption” · `card.everyday_technology.068.c4` (fact): Public-key encryption uses two keys: one locks, and a different one unlocks. / Picture handing out open padlocks: anyone can snap one shut on a box, but only you hold the key that opens it. Public-key cryptography became the backbone of modern internet security, and it lets your browser check that your bank is really who it claims to be. The padlock icon beside a web address signals that your traffic to that site is encrypted.
  - L69 “Passwords and Hacking” · `card.everyday_technology.069.c2` (text): Three common ways in / Phishing: a message with urgent language, a request for your details or a look-alike address such as amazan.com lures you to a fake page. A padlock doesn't prove a site is honest, the FBI warns; phishing sites use HTTPS too. Credential stuffing: username and password pairs leaked in one breach get tried on other sites. Guessing: attackers try common and previously leaked passwords first. None of these needs movie-style genius, just predictable habits.
- **Tested by:**
  - L69 `question.everyday_technology.069.q3`: A phishing page shows Level 68's padlock icon beside its address. What does the padlock actually tell you? → **Only that your traffic to it is encrypted**
  - L70 `question.everyday_technology.070.q5`: From Level 68: in public-key encryption, what can anyone holding your public key do? → **Lock a message that only your private key can open**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Security vendors Progress and DNSFilter explain that the padlock certifies an encrypted connection, not the legitimacy of the site. Sources: https://www.progress.com/blogs/https-and-a-padlock-does-not-mean-a-website-is-secure, https://www.dnsfilter.com/blog/the-dangerous-illusion-of-https-why-the-padlock-isnt-enough

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.microwave_magnetron_frequency`: unverified

> **Claim:** A magnetron inside a microwave oven makes microwaves at about 2,450 megahertz, a field that flips about 2.45 billion times a second.

- **Concept:** How a microwave oven heats food (`concept.everyday_technology.microwave_heating`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L72 “Microwave Ovens” · `card.everyday_technology.072.c2` (text): Twisting water, billions of times a second / The magnetron fills the oven with microwaves at about 2,450 megahertz. Water molecules in food have a slightly negative oxygen end and a slightly positive hydrogen end, and like Level 3's charges, those ends get pushed and pulled. The waves' field flips about 2.45 billion times a second, twisting the molecules back and forth until they jostle their neighbors. That jostling is heat. Level 9's grid current flips 60 times a second. Microwaves are busier.
- **Tested by:**

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. FDA: microwaves are produced by an electron tube called a magnetron. Britannica: about 2,450 megahertz. McGill OSS: water molecules flip back and forth some 2.45 billion times a second. Sources: https://www.mcgill.ca/oss/article/general/device-causes-water-molecules-flip-back-and-forth-some-245-billion-times-second-what-it

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.motion_gas_car_efficiency`: unverified

> **Claim:** Only about 12%-30% of the energy in the fuel put in a conventional car moves it down the road; most of the rest is lost in the engine, mainly as heat.

- **Appears in:**

The difference is mostly heat: an engine burning fuel loses most of its energy that way, and an electric motor loses far less. Level 2's rule does the accounting: less energy lost means more of it moving you.
  - L30 “Checkpoint: Engines and Motion” · `card.everyday_technology.030.c4` (text): One rule under all of them / No machine in this chapter makes energy. A gas engine turns fuel into motion but loses most of it as heat. An electric car loses far less, getting over 77% of its plug energy to the wheels. Levers, gears and hydraulics only reshape a push: more force, paid for with more distance. Horsepower and watts just measure how fast any of them delivers the energy.

Level 25's regenerative braking saves some of that energy as electricity; friction brakes can only turn it into heat.

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.internet_tcp_retransmit`: unverified

> **Claim:** TCP numbers the data it sends, so the receiver can put packets in order and spot gaps; lost packets are detected and sent again.

- **Concept:** TCP/IP: the network of networks (`concept.everyday_technology.internet_tcp_ip`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L62 “Packets” · `card.everyday_technology.062.c4` (fact): Lost packets are simply sent again. / That's the job of the TCP half of Level 61's TCP/IP. TCP numbers the data it sends, so the receiving computer can put packets back in order and spot any gap. When a packet goes missing, it gets sent again. Think of a jigsaw puzzle with numbered pieces: you know exactly which one to ask for.
  - L70 “Checkpoint: The Internet” · `card.everyday_technology.070.c2` (comparison): One message, three stretches: Leaving home (Wi-Fi radio carries it to your router (Level 64); It travels as packets over any available route (Level 62)) vs On the way (Public-key encryption keeps it unreadable (Level 68); TCP numbers the packets and resends lost ones) vs Arriving (The receiver puts the packets back in order; Only the right key unlocks the contents)
- **Tested by:**
  - L62 `question.everyday_technology.062.q3`: Level 61 introduced TCP/IP. What does TCP do when one of a message's packets goes missing? → **Spots the gap and has that packet sent again**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Khan Academy and GeeksforGeeks explain that TCP sequence numbers let the receiver reorder data and detect missing packets, which the sender retransmits. Sources: https://www.khanacademy.org/computing/computers-and-internet/xcae6f4a7ff015e7d:the-internet/xcae6f4a7ff015e7d:transporting-packets/a/transmission-control-protocol--tcp, https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/computer-networks/wrap-around-concept-and-tcp-sequence-number/

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.internet_fiber_1000km`: unverified

> **Claim:** At about 5 millionths of a second per kilometer, 1,000 km of fiber takes about 5 thousandths of a second and 10,000 km about a twentieth of a second, one way.

- **Appears in:**
  - L70 “Checkpoint: The Internet” · `card.everyday_technology.070.c1` (text): Chapter 7 finale: how long does your message take to cross an ocean? / You tap Send. Your words leave by radio, cross the seabed as flashes of laser light in glass fiber and arrive on another continent. Put the whole chapter together and the answer is a small fraction of a second: about a twentieth for 10,000 km of fiber.
  - L70 “Checkpoint: The Internet” · `card.everyday_technology.070.c4` (fact): Every 1,000 km of fiber adds about 5 thousandths of a second. / At 5 millionths of a second per kilometer, 1,000 km takes 5 thousandths of a second, and a 10,000 km trip takes about a twentieth of a second, one way. Physics sets that floor: the light can't go any faster through the glass.

## Riddle solved: Why was Roman concrete so durable? (MIT News)

- **Source:** `source.mit_concrete`
- **URL:** https://news.mit.edu/2023/roman-concrete-durability-lime-casts-0106
- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-24 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.build_lime_clast_test`: unverified

> **Claim:** In the 2023 study, deliberately cracked concrete made by hot mixing healed its cracks within two weeks, while matching concrete made without quicklime did not.

- **Concept:** Roman concrete (`concept.everyday_technology.build_roman_concrete`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L84 “Concrete” · `card.everyday_technology.084.c4` (fact): Rome's Pantheon, almost 1,900 years old, still has the largest unreinforced concrete dome. / No steel bars at all. A 2023 MIT-led study of Roman concrete from another site, Privernum, offers one explanation for such durability: white lumps called lime clasts, formed by mixing with hot quicklime. When a crack reaches one and water gets in, dissolved calcium refills the crack as calcium carbonate. Test concrete made this way sealed its cracks within two weeks. These are findings, not a verdict on every Roman building.
- **Tested by:**
  - L84 `question.everyday_technology.084.q2`: According to the 2023 MIT-led study, how could lime clasts help Roman concrete heal its cracks? → **Water dissolves their calcium, which refills the crack**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Dezeen and the American Ceramic Society report the hot-mixed test samples' cracks sealed within two weeks while control samples kept leaking. Sources: https://www.dezeen.com/2023/01/17/self-healing-roman-concrete-mit-harvard/, https://ceramics.org/ceramic-tech-today/relict-no-more-purposeful-inclusion-of-lime-clasts-gives-roman-concretes-self-healing-properties/

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.flight_lift_both_views`: unverified

> **Claim:** NASA says the pressure (Bernoulli) and flow-turning (Newton) explanations of lift are both correct descriptions of the same force.

- **Concept:** How a wing makes lift (`concept.everyday_technology.flight_lift`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L31 “How Planes Fly” · `card.everyday_technology.031.c3` (text): How a wing really lifts / A wing is shaped and tilted so it turns the passing air downward. By Newton's third law, if the wing pushes air down, the air pushes the wing up. Now look at the same thing as pressure: the air speeds up over the top, and faster air has lower pressure, so the higher pressure underneath pushes up. NASA's point is that these aren't rival theories. Pressure and flow turning are two ways of describing one force: lift.
- **Tested by:**
  - L31 `question.everyday_technology.031.q2`: According to NASA, what is really going on when a wing makes lift? → **It turns air downward, and the air pushes it up**

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Smithsonian How Things Fly describes lift both through pressure difference (Bernoulli) and through wings pushing air down; both presented as valid. Sources: https://howthingsfly.si.edu/aerodynamics/air-motion

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.flight_equal_transit_myth`: unverified

  - L31 “How Planes Fly” · `card.everyday_technology.031.c4` (fact): Air over the top of a wing reaches the back edge first. / So the "meet up at the back" story fails its own test: the air on top doesn't wait for its partner. What matters is the wing's angle to the oncoming air, its angle of attack. Pilots raise the nose at takeoff to get more lift, though tilt too far and the wing stalls.
