### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.transport_newton_third_law`: unverified

> **Claim:** All thrust comes from Newton's third law, for every action an equal and opposite reaction: an engine accelerates a working fluid and the reaction pushes the vehicle.

- **Concept:** Action and reaction push vehicles (`concept.everyday_technology.transport_action_reaction`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L32 “Jet Engines” · `card.everyday_technology.032.c2` (text): Throw air back, get pushed forward / For every action there's an equal and opposite reaction: Newton's third law. Every engine that moves a vehicle uses it. It grabs a working fluid, accelerates it backward, and the reaction pushes the engine forward. A jet's working fluid is the air around it, and it makes thrust because the gas leaves the back faster than the air came in. That push is Level 31's thrust, the force that beats drag.

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.crypto_encryption_def`: unverified

> **Claim:** Encryption uses an algorithm and a key to turn readable plaintext into ciphertext, so only the intended recipient, holding the right key, can read it.

- **Concept:** Encryption basics (`concept.everyday_technology.crypto_encryption_basics`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L68 “Encryption” · `card.everyday_technology.068.c1` (text): Your messages pass through networks you'll never see. / Remember Level 62? Your packets travel over whatever route is available, across many connected networks. So what keeps the computers along the way from reading your bank details? The packets are scrambled, and only the intended recipient can unscramble them.
  - L68 “Encryption” · `card.everyday_technology.068.c2` (text): Scramble it with a key / Encryption uses a method and a key to turn readable plaintext into scrambled ciphertext, so only someone with the right key can read it. Julius Caesar used a simple version: he replaced each letter with the one three places down the alphabet, so HELLO became KHOOR. His key was the number three. It's also easy to crack, because there are only 25 possible shifts to try.
- **Tested by:**
  - L68 `question.everyday_technology.068.q1`: In encryption, what does a key turn readable plaintext into? → **Ciphertext only the right key can read**
  - L68 `question.everyday_technology.068.q3`: Why does Level 62's way of moving packets make encryption so important? → **Packets cross many networks on the way to their destination**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Britannica's Caesar cipher and cryptology entries describe enciphering plaintext into ciphertext with a key that the recipient uses to decipher. Sources: https://www.britannica.com/topic/Caesar-cipher
- **Weak evidence:** one-page (revisit first)

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.crypto_two_keys`: unverified

> **Claim:** Public-key cryptography uses two separate keys: one to encrypt the data and a different one to decrypt it.

- **Concept:** Public-key encryption (`concept.everyday_technology.crypto_public_key`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L68 “Encryption” · `card.everyday_technology.068.c4` (fact): Public-key encryption uses two keys: one locks, and a different one unlocks. / Picture handing out open padlocks: anyone can snap one shut on a box, but only you hold the key that opens it. Public-key cryptography became the backbone of modern internet security, and it lets your browser check that your bank is really who it claims to be. The padlock icon beside a web address signals that your traffic to that site is encrypted.
  - L70 “Checkpoint: The Internet” · `card.everyday_technology.070.c2` (comparison): One message, three stretches: Leaving home (Wi-Fi radio carries it to your router (Level 64); It travels as packets over any available route (Level 62)) vs On the way (Public-key encryption keeps it unreadable (Level 68); TCP numbers the packets and resends lost ones) vs Arriving (The receiver puts the packets back in order; Only the right key unlocks the contents)
- **Tested by:**
  - L69 `question.everyday_technology.069.q3`: A phishing page shows Level 68's padlock icon beside its address. What does the padlock actually tell you? → **Only that your traffic to it is encrypted**
  - L70 `question.everyday_technology.070.q5`: From Level 68: in public-key encryption, what can anyone holding your public key do? → **Lock a message that only your private key can open**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. IBM and the Open University explain asymmetric encryption: anyone can encrypt with the public key, only the matching private key decrypts (the open-padlock analogy). Sources: https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/asymmetric-encryption, https://www.open.edu/openlearn/mod/oucontent/view.php?id=48322&section=1.4

## Putting Einstein to the Test (NIST)

- **Source:** `source.nist_gps_relativity`
- **URL:** https://www.nist.gov/atomic-clocks/a-powerful-tool-for-science/putting-einstein-test
- **License:** US_gov_public_domain · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.gps_relativity_38`: unverified

> **Claim:** GPS satellite clocks run about 38 microseconds a day fast: weaker gravity speeds them 45, orbital speed slows them 7; uncorrected, errors would grow about 10 km a day.

- **Concept:** GPS clocks and relativity (`concept.everyday_technology.gps_clocks`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L37 “GPS” · `card.everyday_technology.037.c4` (fact): GPS satellite clocks run about 38 microseconds a day fast. / That's Einstein's relativity at work. Weaker gravity up there speeds the clocks by about 45 microseconds a day, and their orbital speed slows them by about 7, so engineers built in the correction. Ignore it and position errors would pile up at about 10 kilometers a day. Tiny times matter, because light travels about 300 meters in a millionth of a second.
  - L40 “Checkpoint: Getting Around” · `card.everyday_technology.040.c4` (text): Finding the way: time a wave / The chapter's other trick is a stopwatch. Radar times a radio echo's round trip and halves it. Sonar does the same with sound, which crosses seawater at about 1,500 meters a second. GPS times one-way signals instead, which only works because the satellites carry atomic clocks, corrected for relativity. Distance is speed times time, whether you're a ship, a plane or a phone.
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. GPS World "Inside the box: GPS and relativity" and arXiv gr-qc/0306076 give the same net 38 microseconds per day correction. Sources: https://www.gpsworld.com/inside-the-box-gps-and-relativity/
- **Weak evidence:** one-page (revisit first)

## The International System of Units (SI), NIST Special Publication 330 (2019) (National Institute of Standards and Technology)

- **Source:** `source.nist_sp330_si`
- **URL:** https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.330-2019.pdf

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.ampere_electrons`: unverified

> **Claim:** One ampere is a flow of one coulomb of charge per second, about 6.2 billion billion (6.2 x 10^18) electrons per second.

- **Concept:** Electric current (`concept.everyday_technology.electric_current`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L3 “Electricity” · `card.everyday_technology.003.c3` (fact): Current counts how many electrons pass, not how fast they go. / Current is measured in amperes. One ampere means about 6.2 billion billion electrons passing a point every second. Each one is slow, but there are so many that the flow adds up. And when you close a switch, the push reaches every electron in the circuit at nearly the speed of light, so they all start moving at once. The light doesn't wait.
  - L3 “Electricity” · `card.everyday_technology.003.c4` (text): Voltage is the push / Voltage says how much energy each bit of charge gets. One volt means one joule for every coulomb, the charge one ampere carries in a second. An analogy helps, if you remember it's only a picture: a battery is like the pump that lifts water to the top of a water slide, so it can run back down. A 1.5-volt battery gives each coulomb 1.5 joules for the trip around.
- **Tested by:**
  - L3 `question.everyday_technology.003.q2`: Electrons drift slowly, so why does a lamp light the instant you flip the switch? → **The push reaches every electron almost at once**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. OpenStax: 1 A = 1 C/s. With NIST's exact elementary charge 1.602176634 x 10^-19 C, one coulomb is 6.24 x 10^18 electrons. Sources: https://openstax.org/books/college-physics-2e/pages/20-1-current, https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.330-2019.pdf

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.watt_definition`: unverified

> **Claim:** One watt is one joule per second, so a 60-watt bulb uses 60 joules of energy every second it is on.

- **Concept:** Watts and kilowatt-hours (`concept.everyday_technology.electric_power`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L10 “Checkpoint: Energy and Electricity” · `card.everyday_technology.010.c3` (text): Watts: how fast energy flows / A watt is one joule of energy every second. Remember Level 2's apple? Lifting one a meter every second takes about a watt. Watts also join Level 3's two ideas: volts times amps equals watts, because joules per coulomb times coulombs per second gives joules per second. A 60-watt bulb uses 60 joules every second it's on.
  - L22 “The Steam Engine” · `card.everyday_technology.022.c4` (fact): Level 10's watt is named after James Watt. / A watt is one joule of energy every second: the unit behind Level 10's 60-watt bulb. It honors the engineer whose work made steam engines far less wasteful. So each time you read a bulb's rating, you're quietly crediting a steam engineer.
  - L30 “Checkpoint: Engines and Motion” · `card.everyday_technology.030.c2` (fact): One horsepower is about 746 watts. / Watt defined it as 33,000 foot-pounds of work per minute. In Level 10's units, that's about 746 joules every second. So a 100-horsepower engine delivers about 74,600 watts, or about 75 kilowatts. Two units of power, both from the same man: one named for horses, one named for him.
  - L30 “Checkpoint: Engines and Motion” · `card.everyday_technology.030.c4` (text): One rule under all of them / No machine in this chapter makes energy. A gas engine turns fuel into motion but loses most of it as heat. An electric car loses far less, getting over 77% of its plug energy to the wheels. Levers, gears and hydraulics only reshape a push: more force, paid for with more distance. Horsepower and watts just measure how fast any of them delivers the energy.
- **Tested by:**
  - L10 `question.everyday_technology.010.q1`: What is one watt? → **One joule of energy per second**
  - L10 `question.everyday_technology.010.q2`: A device runs on 10 volts and draws 2 amperes. What is its power? → **20 watts**

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.kilowatt_hour`: unverified

> **Claim:** A kilowatt-hour is 1,000 watts for one hour (3,600 seconds): 3.6 million joules.

- **Concept:** Watts and kilowatt-hours (`concept.everyday_technology.electric_power`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L10 “Checkpoint: Energy and Electricity” · `card.everyday_technology.010.c4` (fact): A kilowatt-hour is 3.6 million joules. / That's 1,000 watts running for an hour (3,600 seconds), and it's the unit utilities measure and charge for. In apples, that's 3.6 million small apples, each lifted a meter. Swap an old bulb for an LED, which uses at least 75% less energy, and the same light takes a quarter or less of the kilowatt-hours.
  - L67 “The Cloud” · `card.everyday_technology.067.c3` (fact): Data centers used about 415 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity in 2024. / That's the IEA's estimate of 415 terawatt-hours, around 1.5% of all the world's electricity. Each of those kilowatt-hours is Level 10's 3.6 million joules. Per unit of floor space, a data center uses 10 to 50 times the energy of a typical office building, says the US Department of Energy.
  - L75 “Heating and Cooling” · `card.everyday_technology.075.c4` (fact): A heat pump can move about 3 kWh of heat indoors using 1 kWh of electricity. / An ordinary electric heater turns each kilowatt-hour, Level 10's unit, into one kilowatt-hour of heat. A heat pump spends its electricity moving heat that already exists, so it can bring in about three. Level 2's rule survives: nothing is created, just transferred. That's why heat pumps are so much more efficient than traditional heating.
  - L96 “Fusion Power” · `card.everyday_technology.096.c4` (fact): NIF's gain was on the target, not the whole facility. / The lasers delivered 2.05 megajoules and fusion released 3.15, a gain above 1.5 on the target. But making each shot takes about 300 megajoules of electricity from the grid, so the facility as a whole used far more energy than the fusion made. By Level 10's math, 3.15 megajoules is under one kilowatt-hour.
- **Tested by:**
  - L67 `question.everyday_technology.067.q3`: The IEA says data centers used 415 terawatt-hours in 2024. In Level 10's billing unit, the kilowatt-hour, how much is that? → **About 415 billion kWh**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. NIST SP 811 B.8: 1 kW h = 3.6 x 10^6 J; Penn State: one kilowatt hour is 3.6 MJ; arithmetic 1,000 x 3,600 = 3.6 million. Sources: https://www.nist.gov/pml/special-publication-811/nist-guide-si-appendix-b-conversion-factors/nist-guide-si-appendix-b8, https://courses.ems.psu.edu/earth104/book/export/html/1344

Your receiver's clock is far cruder, and that's a problem when timing light.   - L37 “GPS” · `card.everyday_technology.037.c2` (text): Distance from a delay / At least 24 GPS satellites circle about 20,200 km up, each going around Earth twice a day, arranged so at least four are in view from almost anywhere. Each one broadcasts its position and the time. Your receiver notes how long each signal took to arrive. The signals travel at the speed of light, so every delay becomes a distance.
  - L40 “Checkpoint: Getting Around” · `card.everyday_technology.040.c4` (text): Finding the way: time a wave / The chapter's other trick is a stopwatch. Radar times a radio echo's round trip and halves it. Sonar does the same with sound, which crosses seawater at about 1,500 meters a second. GPS times one-way signals instead, which only works because the satellites carry atomic clocks, corrected for relativity. Distance is speed times time, whether you're a ship, a plane or a phone.
- **Tested by:**
  - L37 `question.everyday_technology.037.q1`: How does a GPS receiver work out its distance to each satellite? → **From how long the satellite's signal took to arrive**
  - L37 `question.everyday_technology.037.q3`: Level 35's radar times an echo that goes out and back. How is GPS timing different? → **GPS measures a one-way trip the receiver only hears**
  - L40 `question.everyday_technology.040.q5`: Getting Around recap: radar halves its echo time, but GPS does not. Why not? → **A GPS signal only travels one way**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. GPS.gov overview: satellites transmit one-way signals giving position and time, used by receivers to calculate three-dimensional location and time. Sources: https://archive.gps.gov/systems/gps/

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.motion_lever_law`: unverified

> **Claim:** A lever turns on a pivot (fulcrum); force times distance from the fulcrum balances on each side, so an effort five times farther out than the load is multiplied five times.

It's a bar that turns on a pivot, the fulcrum. Its rule: force times distance from the fulcrum balances on each side. ### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.motion_work_tradeoff`: unverified

> **Claim:** A machine cannot do more work than the energy put into it: with 4 supporting strands you pull 4 meters of rope to lift a load 1 meter, and friction takes a little extra.

- **Concept:** Trading force for distance (`concept.everyday_technology.motion_mechanical_advantage`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L21 “Levers, Wheels and Pulleys” · `card.everyday_technology.021.c4` (fact): No machine gives you free work. / The extra force always costs distance. With 4 strands holding the load, you have to haul in 4 meters of rope to lift it 1 meter. Force times distance, the work, comes out the same, and friction takes a little extra on top. Level 2's rule again: energy is never created, not even by Archimedes.
  - L27 “Gears” · `card.everyday_technology.027.c3` (text): Slower, but stronger / That slower gear also turns with twice the twisting force, called torque. It's Level 21's wheel and axle again: gears multiply force by the ratio of their sizes, like levers that go round. Flip the pair, with a big gear driving a small one, and you get speed instead of force. Either way, Level 21's rule holds: no gear hands out free energy.
  - L30 “Checkpoint: Engines and Motion” · `card.everyday_technology.030.c3` (comparison): Engines and motion: three ways to move: Heat into motion (Steam pushes a piston (Level 22); Fuel burns inside the cylinder (Level 24)) vs Electricity into motion (A battery-powered motor turns the wheels (Level 25); Braking can turn motion back into charge) vs Force traded for distance (Levers and pulleys (Level 21), gears (Level 27); A bigger piston, a bigger push (Level 28))
  - L30 “Checkpoint: Engines and Motion” · `card.everyday_technology.030.c4` (text): One rule under all of them / No machine in this chapter makes energy. A gas engine turns fuel into motion but loses most of it as heat. An electric car loses far less, getting over 77% of its plug energy to the wheels. Levers, gears and hydraulics only reshape a push: more force, paid for with more distance. Horsepower and watts just measure how fast any of them delivers the energy.
- **Tested by:**
  - L21 `question.everyday_technology.021.q3`: Level 2 said energy can't be created. How does a pulley system that cuts your pulling force obey that rule? → **You pull more rope, so the work stays the same**
  - L30 `question.everyday_technology.030.q4`: Engines and Motion recap: what do a pulley system, a pair of gears and a hydraulic lift have in common? → **They multiply force but cost extra distance**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. The Physics Classroom and TeachEngineering both explain that simple machines reduce force but increase distance, with work in at least equal to work out. Sources: https://www.teachengineering.org/lessons/cub_simple_lesson05
- **Weak evidence:** one-page (revisit first)

## Real-World Relativity: The GPS Navigation System (Ohio State University Department of Astronomy)

- **Source:** `source.osu_gps_relativity`
- **URL:** https://www.astronomy.ohio-state.edu/pogge.1/Ast162/Unit5/gps.html
- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.gps_relativity_38`: unverified

> **Claim:** GPS satellite clocks run about 38 microseconds a day fast: weaker gravity speeds them 45, orbital speed slows them 7; uncorrected, errors would grow about 10 km a day.

- **Concept:** GPS clocks and relativity (`concept.everyday_technology.gps_clocks`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L37 “GPS” · `card.everyday_technology.037.c4` (fact): GPS satellite clocks run about 38 microseconds a day fast. / That's Einstein's relativity at work. Weaker gravity up there speeds the clocks by about 45 microseconds a day, and their orbital speed slows them by about 7, so engineers built in the correction. Ignore it and position errors would pile up at about 10 kilometers a day. Tiny times matter, because light travels about 300 meters in a millionth of a second.
  - L40 “Checkpoint: Getting Around” · `card.everyday_technology.040.c4` (text): Finding the way: time a wave / The chapter's other trick is a stopwatch. Radar times a radio echo's round trip and halves it. Sonar does the same with sound, which crosses seawater at about 1,500 meters a second. GPS times one-way signals instead, which only works because the satellites carry atomic clocks, corrected for relativity. Distance is speed times time, whether you're a ship, a plane or a phone.
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. GPS World "Inside the box: GPS and relativity" and arXiv gr-qc/0306076 give the same net 38 microseconds per day correction. Sources: https://www.gpsworld.com/inside-the-box-gps-and-relativity/
- **Weak evidence:** one-page (revisit first)

```sh
npm run verify:record -- fact.everyday_technology.gps_relativity_38 source.osu_gps_relativity --status verified --by "Your Name" --quote "…"
```

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.battery_dies`: unverified

> **Claim:** A battery stops working when its reacting chemicals are used up; a rechargeable one is restored by driving current through it in reverse, which runs the reaction backward and stores chemical energy again.

Level 3 showed they were in the wires all along; the battery supplies the energy. It dies when its reacting chemicals are used up. Recharging pushes current through it in reverse, running the reaction backward and storing chemical energy again. A charger is really a re-energizer.
  - L10 “Checkpoint: Energy and Electricity” · `card.everyday_technology.010.c2` (comparison): Electricity: made, stored, used: Made (Generators spin a magnet inside coils (Level 8); Turbines turn most of them) vs Stored (Batteries hold chemical energy (Level 6); Recharging runs the reaction backward) vs Used (Bulbs turn it into light and heat (Level 5); Motors turn it into motion (Level 7))
  - L49 “What's Inside a Smartphone” · `card.everyday_technology.049.c4` (fact): The battery is a lithium-ion cell, a Nobel Prize-winning design. / Lithium-ion batteries are light, rechargeable and powerful, which is why they run phones and laptops. Level 6's rule still applies: charging drives current through the battery in reverse, running the reaction backward to store energy again. The chips that run it all get their own chapter.

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.wire_electrons_already_there`: unverified

> **Claim:** The charge carriers in a wire are electrons belonging to the wire's own atoms; a battery supplies energy, not charge, and charge is not used up in a circuit.

- **Concept:** Electric current (`concept.everyday_technology.electric_current`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L3 “Electricity” · `card.everyday_technology.003.c2` (text): Electricity is charge on the move / Atoms hold positive protons and negative electrons. Opposite charges attract; like charges push apart. In a metal wire, when electrons all drift the same way, that's an electric current. And those electrons were in the wire all along, belonging to its own atoms. A wire isn't an empty pipe waiting to be filled. It comes already full.
  - L4 “Circuits” · `card.everyday_technology.004.c2` (text): A circuit is a closed loop / Every circuit has three parts: a source of energy such as a battery, something that uses the current such as a bulb, and wires joining them. The loop has to run unbroken from one end of the battery, through the bulb, back to the other end. In a single loop, a break anywhere stops the current everywhere. Remember Level 3: the electrons are already in the wire. The loop lets them all move.
  - L6 “Batteries” · `card.everyday_technology.006.c4` (text): "Dead" doesn't mean empty / A flat battery hasn't run out of electrons. Level 3 showed they were in the wires all along; the battery supplies the energy. It dies when its reacting chemicals are used up. Recharging pushes current through it in reverse, running the reaction backward and storing chemical energy again. A charger is really a re-energizer.
  - L10 “Checkpoint: Energy and Electricity” · `card.everyday_technology.010.c1` (text): Chapter 1 finale: what does your electricity bill actually charge for? / Not electrons: Level 3 showed they were in your wires all along. You pay for energy, measured in kilowatt-hours. To see what that means, put the whole chapter together.
- **Tested by:**
  - L3 `question.everyday_technology.003.q1`: What is an electric current? → **Charge moving through a wire**
  - L4 `question.everyday_technology.004.q3`: Level 3 said a wire is already full of electrons. So why won't a bulb light when there's a gap in the wire? → **Without a closed loop, the charge can't flow around**
  - L7 `question.everyday_technology.007.q3`: Magnetic poles behave much like Level 3's electric charges. In what way? → **Opposites attract and likes push apart**
  - L46 `question.everyday_technology.046.q3`: Level 3 said a current is moving charge. What does light do when it strikes a pixel on a digital camera's sensor? → **It induces a small electric current**
  - L96 `question.everyday_technology.096.q3`: Level 3 said like charges repel. Why does that make fusion so hard? → **Positively charged nuclei push each other apart**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. OpenStax 20.1 explains that charge entering one end of a wire pushes an equal amount out the other; the carriers are the conductor's free electrons. Sources: https://openstax.org/books/college-physics-2e/pages/20-1-current
- **Weak evidence:** one-page (revisit first)

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.closed_loop`: unverified

> **Claim:** Current flows only around a closed conducting loop from one terminal of the source to the other; a break anywhere in a single loop stops the current everywhere in it.

- **Concept:** Circuits and switches (`concept.everyday_technology.circuit_closed_loop`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L4 “Circuits” · `card.everyday_technology.004.c1` (text): Wire a kitchen as one chain, and the fridge only runs while the toaster is on. / That would make breakfast awkward. Real kitchens aren't wired that way, and the reason comes from the same idea that makes every light switch work: electricity only flows around a complete loop.
  - L4 “Circuits” · `card.everyday_technology.004.c2` (text): A circuit is a closed loop / Every circuit has three parts: a source of energy such as a battery, something that uses the current such as a bulb, and wires joining them. The loop has to run unbroken from one end of the battery, through the bulb, back to the other end. In a single loop, a break anywhere stops the current everywhere. Remember Level 3: the electrons are already in the wire. The loop lets them all move.
  - L6 “Batteries” · `card.everyday_technology.006.c3` (text): What's inside every battery / A battery turns chemical energy into electrical energy. It has two ends, the anode and the cathode, with an electrolyte between them. Electrons leave the anode, travel around the outside circuit and arrive at the cathode, while charged particles called ions move through the electrolyte inside to balance them. Remember Level 4: nothing flows until the loop is closed. A common cell gives about 1.5 volts.
- **Tested by:**
  - L4 `question.everyday_technology.004.q3`: Level 3 said a wire is already full of electrons. So why won't a bulb light when there's a gap in the wire? → **Without a closed loop, the charge can't flow around**
  - L6 `question.everyday_technology.006.q3`: Level 4 said current needs a closed loop. Where do electrons go after leaving a battery's anode? → **Around the outside circuit to the cathode**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Britannica describes a circuit as a complete path; The Physics Classroom's series page notes that cutting current to one part of a single path cuts it to all. Sources: https://www.britannica.com/technology/electric-circuit, https://www.physicsclassroom.com/class/circuits/lesson-4/two-types-of-connections

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.conductors_insulators`: unverified

> **Claim:** Metals such as copper are conductors that carry charge easily; materials like paper and plastic are insulators that stop the flow.

- **Concept:** Circuits and switches (`concept.everyday_technology.circuit_closed_loop`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L4 “Circuits” · `card.everyday_technology.004.c3` (text): A switch is a gap you control / Metals such as copper are conductors: charge moves through them easily. Paper and plastic are insulators, and they stop the flow. A switch in the "off" position opens a gap in the loop, so no current can flow. "On" closes the gap and completes the loop. It sounds backwards, but in a circuit, closed means go.
  - L49 “What's Inside a Smartphone” · `card.everyday_technology.049.c2` (text): The screen that feels your finger / Most smartphones have capacitive touchscreens. The screen carries an electric field, and your finger, which conducts electricity, disturbs that field by an amount that depends on where it is. The phone works out the spot, and it can track several fingers at once. A plain plastic stylus does nothing, because plastic is an insulator, Level 4's word for a material that stops the flow of charge.

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.wire_electrons_already_there`: unverified

> **Claim:** The charge carriers in a wire are electrons belonging to the wire's own atoms; a battery supplies energy, not charge, and charge is not used up in a circuit.

- **Appears in:**
  - L3 “Electricity” · `card.everyday_technology.003.c2` (text): Electricity is charge on the move / Atoms hold positive protons and negative electrons. Opposite charges attract; like charges push apart. In a metal wire, when electrons all drift the same way, that's an electric current. And those electrons were in the wire all along, belonging to its own atoms. A wire isn't an empty pipe waiting to be filled. It comes already full.
  - L4 “Circuits” · `card.everyday_technology.004.c2` (text): A circuit is a closed loop / Every circuit has three parts: a source of energy such as a battery, something that uses the current such as a bulb, and wires joining them. The loop has to run unbroken from one end of the battery, through the bulb, back to the other end. In a single loop, a break anywhere stops the current everywhere. Remember Level 3: the electrons are already in the wire. The loop lets them all move.
  - L6 “Batteries” · `card.everyday_technology.006.c4` (text): "Dead" doesn't mean empty / A flat battery hasn't run out of electrons. Level 3 showed they were in the wires all along; the battery supplies the energy. It dies when its reacting chemicals are used up. Recharging pushes current through it in reverse, running the reaction backward and storing chemical energy again. A charger is really a re-energizer.
  - L10 “Checkpoint: Energy and Electricity” · `card.everyday_technology.010.c1` (text): Chapter 1 finale: what does your electricity bill actually charge for? / Not electrons: Level 3 showed they were in your wires all along. You pay for energy, measured in kilowatt-hours. To see what that means, put the whole chapter together.

  - L7 `question.everyday_technology.007.q3`: Magnetic poles behave much like Level 3's electric charges. In what way? → **Opposites attract and likes push apart**
  - L46 `question.everyday_technology.046.q3`: Level 3 said a current is moving charge. What does light do when it strikes a pixel on a digital camera's sensor? → **It induces a small electric current**
  - L96 `question.everyday_technology.096.q3`: Level 3 said like charges repel. Why does that make fusion so hard? → **Positively charged nuclei push each other apart**

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.watt_definition`: unverified

> **Claim:** One watt is one joule per second, so a 60-watt bulb uses 60 joules of energy every second it is on.

- **Concept:** Watts and kilowatt-hours (`concept.everyday_technology.electric_power`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L10 “Checkpoint: Energy and Electricity” · `card.everyday_technology.010.c3` (text): Watts: how fast energy flows / A watt is one joule of energy every second. Remember Level 2's apple? Lifting one a meter every second takes about a watt. Watts also join Level 3's two ideas: volts times amps equals watts, because joules per coulomb times coulombs per second gives joules per second. A 60-watt bulb uses 60 joules every second it's on.
  - L22 “The Steam Engine” · `card.everyday_technology.022.c4` (fact): Level 10's watt is named after James Watt. / A watt is one joule of energy every second: the unit behind Level 10's 60-watt bulb. It honors the engineer whose work made steam engines far less wasteful. So each time you read a bulb's rating, you're quietly crediting a steam engineer.
  - L30 “Checkpoint: Engines and Motion” · `card.everyday_technology.030.c2` (fact): One horsepower is about 746 watts. / Watt defined it as 33,000 foot-pounds of work per minute. In Level 10's units, that's about 746 joules every second. So a 100-horsepower engine delivers about 74,600 watts, or about 75 kilowatts. Two units of power, both from the same man: one named for horses, one named for him.
  - L30 “Checkpoint: Engines and Motion” · `card.everyday_technology.030.c4` (text): One rule under all of them / No machine in this chapter makes energy. A gas engine turns fuel into motion but loses most of it as heat. An electric car loses far less, getting over 77% of its plug energy to the wheels. Levers, gears and hydraulics only reshape a push: more force, paid for with more distance. Horsepower and watts just measure how fast any of them delivers the energy.

## A Bicycle Can Be Self-Stable Without Gyroscopic or Caster Effects (Science (AAAS), 2011)

- **Source:** `source.science_kooijman_2011_bicycle`

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.motion_bike_common_view`: unverified

> **Claim:** The common explanation for self-steering credited gyroscopic effects of the spinning front wheel or trail, the front contact point trailing behind the steering axis like a caster.

- **Concept:** Why some bikes balance themselves (`concept.everyday_technology.motion_bike_self_stability`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L29 “Why Bicycles Stay Up” · `card.everyday_technology.029.c3` (text): A bike that balances itself / Give a riderless bike a push at a decent speed and it can roll along upright, recovering from a sideways shove. As it leans, its front wheel steers into the lean all by itself. The usual explanation credited two things: the gyroscopic effect of the spinning front wheel, and trail, the way the front wheel touches the ground behind the steering axis, like a shopping-cart caster.
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. ScienceDaily (Cornell release) calls the gyro and caster effects the long-accepted explanations. Sources: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2011/04/110414141356.htm

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.motion_bike_self_stable`: unverified

> **Claim:** A riderless bicycle moving fast enough steers itself into a lean and recovers from a sideways push; the 2011 test bike did this above about 5 mph (8 km/h).

- **Concept:** Why some bikes balance themselves (`concept.everyday_technology.motion_bike_self_stability`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L29 “Why Bicycles Stay Up” · `card.everyday_technology.029.c3` (text): A bike that balances itself / Give a riderless bike a push at a decent speed and it can roll along upright, recovering from a sideways shove. As it leans, its front wheel steers into the lean all by itself. The usual explanation credited two things: the gyroscopic effect of the spinning front wheel, and trail, the way the front wheel touches the ground behind the steering axis, like a shopping-cart caster.
  - L29 “Why Bicycles Stay Up” · `card.everyday_technology.029.c4` (fact): In 2011, a bike with neither effect still balanced itself. / Kooijman and colleagues built a bike with extra wheels spinning backwards to cancel the gyroscopic effect, and a front wheel touching down ahead of the steering axis, so no trail. Rolling above about 5 mph (8 km/h), it still steered itself upright (Science, 2011). Where the bike's mass sits matters too. The honest summary: it's a mix of effects, and researchers say much is still to be learned.
- **Tested by:**

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.flight_lift_pressure`: unverified

> **Claim:** A wing is shaped and tilted so air over it moves faster than air under it; faster air has lower pressure, so the wing is pushed up.

- **Concept:** How a wing makes lift (`concept.everyday_technology.flight_lift`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L31 “How Planes Fly” · `card.everyday_technology.031.c3` (text): How a wing really lifts / A wing is shaped and tilted so it turns the passing air downward. By Newton's third law, if the wing pushes air down, the air pushes the wing up. Now look at the same thing as pressure: the air speeds up over the top, and faster air has lower pressure, so the higher pressure underneath pushes up. NASA's point is that these aren't rival theories. Pressure and flow turning are two ways of describing one force: lift.
- **Tested by:**
  - L31 `question.everyday_technology.031.q2`: According to NASA, what is really going on when a wing makes lift? → **It turns air downward, and the air pushes it up**

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. NASA Glenn "Bernoulli and Newton": Bernoulli's equation relates pressure to local velocity, and integrating pressure around the wing gives the lift force. Sources: https://www1.grc.nasa.gov/beginners-guide-to-aeronautics/bernoulli-and-newton

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.telegraph_cooke_wheatstone`: unverified

> **Claim:** In 1837 Britain's William Cooke and Charles Wheatstone patented a telegraph with six wires and five needles; the current swung the needles to point at letters, using Oersted's discovery.

- **Concept:** The electric telegraph (`concept.everyday_technology.telegraph_pulses`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L42 “The Telegraph” · `card.everyday_technology.042.c4` (fact): Britain built a telegraph too: Cooke and Wheatstone patented theirs in 1837. / Their instrument used six wires and five needles. The current swung the needles to point at letters, the same effect that moved Ørsted's compass needle in Level 7. Two countries, two designs, one idea: a message can travel as pulses of electric current.

- **Concept:** Trading force for distance (`concept.everyday_technology.motion_mechanical_advantage`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L21 “Levers, Wheels and Pulleys” · `card.everyday_technology.021.c4` (fact): No machine gives you free work. / The extra force always costs distance. With 4 strands holding the load, you have to haul in 4 meters of rope to lift it 1 meter. Force times distance, the work, comes out the same, and friction takes a little extra on top. Level 2's rule again: energy is never created, not even by Archimedes.
  - L27 “Gears” · `card.everyday_technology.027.c3` (text): Slower, but stronger / That slower gear also turns with twice the twisting force, called torque. It's Level 21's wheel and axle again: gears multiply force by the ratio of their sizes, like levers that go round. Flip the pair, with a big gear driving a small one, and you get speed instead of force. Either way, Level 21's rule holds: no gear hands out free energy.
  - L30 “Checkpoint: Engines and Motion” · `card.everyday_technology.030.c3` (comparison): Engines and motion: three ways to move: Heat into motion (Steam pushes a piston (Level 22); Fuel burns inside the cylinder (Level 24)) vs Electricity into motion (A battery-powered motor turns the wheels (Level 25); Braking can turn motion back into charge) vs Force traded for distance (Levers and pulleys (Level 21), gears (Level 27); A bigger piston, a bigger push (Level 28))
  - L30 “Checkpoint: Engines and Motion” · `card.everyday_technology.030.c4` (text): One rule under all of them / No machine in this chapter makes energy. A gas engine turns fuel into motion but loses most of it as heat. An electric car loses far less, getting over 77% of its plug energy to the wheels. Levers, gears and hydraulics only reshape a push: more force, paid for with more distance. Horsepower and watts just measure how fast any of them delivers the energy.
- **Tested by:**
  - L21 `question.everyday_technology.021.q3`: Level 2 said energy can't be created. How does a pulley system that cuts your pulling force obey that rule? → **You pull more rope, so the work stays the same**
  - L30 `question.everyday_technology.030.q4`: Engines and Motion recap: what do a pulley system, a pair of gears and a hydraulic lift have in common? → **They multiply force but cost extra distance**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. The Physics Classroom and TeachEngineering both explain that simple machines reduce force but increase distance, with work in at least equal to work out. Sources: https://www.teachengineering.org/lessons/cub_simple_lesson05

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.telegraph_how`: unverified

> **Claim:** In Morse's telegraph a key made and broke the circuit; at the receiver an electromagnet, switched on and off by the signals, moved a stylus that marked dots (short signals) and dashes (longer ones) on moving paper.

- **Appears in:**
  - L42 “The Telegraph” · `card.everyday_technology.042.c2` (text): A switch at one end, a magnet at the other / A telegraph is Level 4's circuit stretched between cities. The sender's key is a switch: press it and the loop closes, so current flows; let go and it opens. At the far end, that current switches an electromagnet on and off, just like the ones in Level 7. In Morse's system the magnet pulled a stylus that marked a moving strip of paper. A short signal made a dot, a longer one a dash.
  - L43 “The Telephone” · `card.everyday_technology.043.c2` (text): A current shaped like your voice / Level 42's telegraph only switched current on and off. A telephone does something subtler. Your voice makes a thin diaphragm vibrate, and the transmitter turns those vibrations into a current that rises and falls like the sound wave itself. At the other end, the changing current drives an electromagnet that shakes a second diaphragm, rebuilding the sound. The wire carries a copy of your voice, drawn in electricity.
  - L50 “Milestone: Energy to Information” · `card.everyday_technology.050.c3` (text): Same electricity, two jobs / Power is about how much energy flows. A signal is about the pattern. ### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.build_disassembly_inspiration`: unverified

> **Claim:** Ford's engineers adapted the "disassembly line" that slaughterhouses used to take carcasses apart step by step, running the idea in reverse to build cars.

- **Concept:** The moving assembly line (`concept.everyday_technology.build_moving_assembly_line`)
- **Appears in:**

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.fridge_moves_heat_out`: unverified

> **Claim:** A refrigerator takes heat from its cold inside and releases it into the room, so the area behind a running fridge feels warmer than the room.

- **Concept:** A fridge moves heat (`concept.everyday_technology.fridge_moves_heat`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L71 “Refrigerators” · `card.everyday_technology.071.c1` (text): Leave the fridge door open on a hot day, and your kitchen gets warmer. / It sounds backwards: all that cold air spilling out. But a fridge doesn't make cold. It moves heat, and that heat has to go somewhere. Put your hand behind a running fridge and you'll feel exactly where.
  - L71 “Refrigerators” · `card.everyday_technology.071.c2` (text): A fridge is a heat mover / Heat never flows on its own from somewhere cold to somewhere warmer. A fridge forces it to. It takes heat out of the cold box and releases it into your kitchen, which is why the area behind a running fridge feels warmer than the room. The inside gets colder because heat left, not because cold arrived. Your fridge is less a cooler than a bouncer, showing heat the door.
  - L75 “Heating and Cooling” · `card.everyday_technology.075.c2` (text): An air conditioner is a fridge for your house / Remember Level 71: a fridge moves heat out of a box and releases it into your kitchen. An air conditioner works on the same principle with a bigger box, your home. Refrigerant soaks up heat indoors and gives it up outside. In this version, your living room is the inside of the fridge, and the whole outdoors is the kitchen.
  - L80 “Checkpoint: Home and Health” · `card.everyday_technology.080.c2` (comparison): Two jobs in one chapter: Moving heat (A fridge pumps heat out of a box (Level 71); A heat pump moves heat either way (Level 75); A microwave makes heat inside the food (Level 72)) vs Fighting germs (Water plants filter and disinfect (Level 73); Sewage plants use microbes, then disinfect (Level 74); Vaccines train your immune system (Level 76))
- **Tested by:**
  - L71 `question.everyday_technology.071.q1`: Where does the heat taken out of a refrigerator's cold compartment go? → **It is released into the kitchen**
  - L75 `question.everyday_technology.075.q3`: Level 71's fridge moves heat out of a cold box. In an air-conditioned house, what plays the part of that cold box? → **The rooms of the house**
  - L80 `question.everyday_technology.080.q4`: Home and Health checkpoint: what job do a fridge, an air conditioner and a heat pump all do? → **Move heat from one place to another**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. HyperPhysics: the refrigerator takes energy from the freezing compartment and exhausts it to the room; the area behind it is warmer. UIUC Physics Van: heat is blown out the back, which is warm while the unit runs. Sources: https://van.physics.illinois.edu/ask/listing/1790, https://www.physlink.com/education/askexperts/ae149.cfm

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.hydro_how`: unverified

> **Claim:** At a hydroelectric dam, water stored in the reservoir enters an intake near the bottom of the dam, falls through a pipe called a penstock, and turns a turbine whose shaft drives a generator.

- **Appears in:**
  - L15 “Hydropower” · `card.everyday_technology.015.c2` (text): How a dam makes electricity / A dam holds back a reservoir of water. Near the bottom of the dam, water enters an intake and falls through a pipe called a penstock. At the end it spins a turbine, and the turbine's shaft turns a generator. No fire, no steam: the water pushes the turbine itself. It's Level 2's gravitational energy, the energy stored in anything raised high, cashed in.

### ☐ `fact.everyday_technology.computer_fetch_decode_execute`: unverified

> **Claim:** From start-up to shutdown, a CPU repeats the instruction cycle: fetch the next instruction from memory, decode what it means, execute it.

- **Appears in:**
  - L60 “Checkpoint: Computers” · `card.everyday_technology.060.c3` (text): Fetch, decode, execute, repeat / Inside the processor, one loop runs from start-up to shutdown. Fetch: the control unit pulls the next instruction from memory. Decode: it works out what the instruction means. Execute: it carries it out, often a sum or a comparison in the arithmetic-logic unit. Then it fetches the next one. Every app you've ever used is that loop, run over and over.

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Wikipedia (Instruction cycle) and Baeldung: the CPU follows the fetch-decode-execute cycle from boot-up until shutdown. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instruction_cycle, https://www.baeldung.com/cs/fetch-execute-cycle
